19.explanation: "Although" correctly introduces the concessive clause contrasting with her refusal (C).

20.q: The old woman walked carefully with her heavy load ______ she should fall.
20.explanation: "Lest" means "for fear that", fitting the careful walking to avoid falling (D).

21.q: They _______ English fluently.
21.explanation: Plural subject "They" takes the base form "speak" (A).

22.q: I ______ to music now.
22.explanation: Present continuous "am listening" matches "now" (D).

23.q: They _____ to the movies last night.
23.explanation: "Last night" signals simple past "went" (B).

25.q: They _____ to the beach every morning.
25.explanation: "Every morning" signals simple present with plural "They": "go" (A).

26.q: Neither Sanga nor his friends ______coming.
26.explanation: "Neither...nor" takes the verb form agreeing with the nearer subject "friends" (plural), so "are" (B).

27.q: She is not as ________ as her sister.
27.explanation: "As...as" requires the positive degree "tall" (A).

28.q: She has been working here _________ five years.
28.explanation: "For" is used with a duration of time (C).

29.q: If she had remembered to set her alarm, she ________ on time now.
29.explanation: Mixed conditional: past perfect in the if-clause with "would have + past participle" in the main clause (B).

30.q: ________ the heavy rain, the match continued without interruption.
30.explanation: "In spite of" is the correct prepositional phrase meaning despite (A).

31.q: The new employee was very ______ to learn.
31.explanation: "Eager to learn" is the standard phrase showing willingness (B).

32.q: The manager asked the boxer to _______ the challenge.
32.explanation: "Accept the challenge" means to take it on (A).

33.q: The company’s ________ objective is to increase sales.
33.explanation: "Principal" as an adjective means main/primary (B).

34.q: This new medicine does not have any side ________.
34.explanation: "Side effects" is the standard plural form (B).

35.q: The _______ we walked, the more beautiful the scenery became.
35.explanation: The comparative structure "the farther...the more" shows increasing distance (A).

36.q: She spoke so softly, her words were almost _________.
36.explanation: "Inaudible" means not able to be heard (C).

37.q: The new law aims to curb practices that are _______ to the environment.
37.explanation: "Detrimental to" means harmful to (A).

38.q: His argument was so ________ that even the skeptics were forced to reconsider their stance.
38.explanation: "Compelling" means convincing or forceful, fitting the skeptics' reaction (B).

39.q: The young prodigy impressed everyone with her _______ grasp of advanced calculus.
39.explanation: "Profound" means deep, fitting "grasp of advanced calculus" (D).

40.q: Despite his __________ behaviour, everyone admired his honesty.
40.explanation: "Amiable" means friendly and pleasant, contrasting with but still admired for honesty (B).

41.q: The police was questioning the accused yesterday.

opts.a: The accused was questioning the police yesterday.
opts.b: The accused was questioned by the police yesterday.
opts.c: The accused were questioned by the police yesterday.
opts.d: The accused was being questioned by the police yesterday.

41.explanation: Simple past passive: "was questioned by" (B).

42.q: She had eaten the fruits yesterday.

opts.a: The fruits have been eaten by her yesterday.
opts.b: The fruits were eaten by her yesterday.
opts.c: The fruits had been eaten by her yesterday.
opts.d: The fruits will be eaten by her yesterday.

42.explanation: Simple past passive: "were eaten by" (B).

43.q: She will not finish the task.

opts.a: The task is not finished by her.
opts.b: The task will not be finished by her.
opts.c: The task was not finished by her.
opts.d: The task will not have been finished by her.

43.explanation: Simple future passive: "will not be finished by" (B).

44.q: Who is bothering you?

opts.d: By whom are you being bothered?

44.explanation: Passive of "Who is bothering you?" becomes "By whom are you being bothered?" (D).

45.q: Hmuifang has been visited by many tourists.

opts.a: Many tourists have been visiting Hmuifang.
opts.d: A number of tourists have visited Hmuifang.

45.explanation: Present perfect active: "have visited" matches "has been visited by" (C).

46.q: He said to me, “I don’t believe you.”

opts.a: He said he didn’t believe me.
opts.b: He said I don’t believe you.
opts.c: He said he don’t believe me.
opts.d: He said I didn’t believe you.

46.explanation: Reported speech: present "don't" becomes past "didn't", and "you" becomes "me" (A).

47.q: She said to me “Where are you going for the vacation?”

opts.a: She said that where I was going for the vacation.
opts.b: She asked where I was going for the vacation
opts.c: She asked me that where I was going for the vacation.
opts.d: She asked where I had gone for the vacation

47.explanation: "Asked where I was going" correctly backshifts the direct question without "that" (B).

49.q: The boy requested his father to forgive him that time.

opts.b: The boy prayed, “Forgive me this once”.
opts.c: The boy said, “Please forgive me father”.
opts.d: The boy said, “Father! Forgive me this time.”

49.explanation: "Requested his father to forgive him" converts to direct speech as "Please forgive me, father" (C).

50.q: He said to me, “Trust in God and do the right.”

opts.a: He advised me to trust in God and do the right.
opts.b: He requested that I trust in God to do the right.
opts.c: He said to trust in God and do the right.
opts.d: He professed to trust in God and do the right.

50.explanation: Reported speech with imperative becomes "He advised me to..." (A).

51.q: What type of sentence is used to ask a question?
51.explanation: Interrogative sentences ask questions (C).

52.q: Changing the sentence The child grows so fast into exclamatory sentence would be:

opts.b: How fast does the child grow.
opts.d: Is the child growing or what?

52.explanation: Exclamatory form of "The child grows so fast" is "How fast the child grows!" (A).

53.q: Changing the sentence Brutus did not hate Caesar into assertive sentence would be:
53.explanation: Removing negation from "Brutus did not hate Caesar" gives the assertive "Brutus loved Caesar" (A).

54.q: What kind of sentence is “This is Sparta!”?
54.explanation: "This is Sparta!" is an exclamatory sentence (C).

55.q: Changing the sentence Man is mortal into a negative sentence would be:
55.explanation: Negative of "Man is mortal" replaces mortal with its opposite: "Man is not immortal" (C).

56.q: What kind of sentence is “Gambling is a bad habit.”?
56.explanation: "Gambling is a bad habit." is a simple sentence (A).

57.q: What kind of sentence is “May you live a hundred years!”?
57.explanation: "May you live a hundred years!" expresses a wish, making it optative (B).

58.q: Changing the sentence, The father said to his son, “Don’t do like that.” into indirect speech would be:

opts.a: The father requested his son to do like that.
opts.b: The father proposed to his son to do like that.
opts.c: The father asked his son to do like that.
opts.d: The father forbade his son to do like that.

58.explanation: Indirect speech of "Don't do like that" becomes "forbade his son to do like that" (D).

59.q: Which of the following is an Imperative sentence?
59.explanation: "Close the door behind you" is a command, making it imperative (B).

60.q: Which of the following is a Declarative sentence?
60.explanation: "My book is missing" is a declarative sentence making a statement (C).

1.q:
Write an essay on any one of the following topics (10 marks):
(a) The detrimental effects of social media.
(b) The impact of Artificial Intelligence.
(c) Cyber-Crime: A Growing Threat.
1.explanation: Choose one topic. Develop a clear introduction, organized supporting points and a conclusion; use relevant examples and accurate language. The printed paper assigns 10 marks.

2.q:
Write a précis of the following passage by reducing it to one third of its length (10 marks):

Reading is one of the most valuable habits a person can develop. It opens up new worlds, ideas, and perspectives, enriching the mind and imagination. Through books, articles, and other written materials, people gain knowledge about history, science, culture, and human behaviour. Reading also improves language skills, vocabulary, and critical thinking. It encourages curiosity and creativity, allowing individuals to explore concepts beyond their immediate experiences. Furthermore, reading can be a source of relaxation and stress relief, offering an escape from the pressures of daily life. In a world full of distractions, dedicating time to reading helps cultivate discipline and focus. Societies that encourage reading tend to be more informed, empathetic, and innovative. Thus, reading is not merely a pastime but a lifelong tool for personal growth and societal advancement.
2.explanation: Write a concise précis of about one third the passage’s length in your own words. Preserve its central ideas: reading builds knowledge, language and critical thinking; supports curiosity, focus and relaxation; and contributes to personal and social growth. Give it a suitable title and avoid adding opinions.

3.q: You are Mr. XYZ living in MINECO. Write a letter of complaint to the Mayor, Aizawl Municipal Corporation regarding the lack of sufficient street lights in your area which has drawn antisocial elements and has increased criminal activities in your neighbourhood (10 marks).
3.explanation: Use a formal letter format with sender’s address, date, recipient and subject. Explain the shortage of street lights and its safety consequences, request prompt installation or repair, and close courteously. The printed paper assigns 10 marks.

4.q:
Read the following passage and answer the questions based on it:

Studies serve for delight, for ornament, and for ability. Their chief use for delight is in privateness and retiring; for ornament is in this course; and for ability is in the judgment and disposition of business. For expert men can execute, and perhaps judge of particulars, one by one; but the general counsels, and the plots and marshalling of affairs, come best, from those that are learned. To spend too much time in studies is sloth; to use them too much for ornaments is affectation; to make judgement wholly by their rules, is the humour of a scholar. They perfect nature, and are perfected by experience: for natural abilities are like natural plants that need pruning, by study; and studies themselves do give forth directions too much at large, except they be bounded in by experience. Crafty men condemn studies, simple men admire them, and wise men use them; for they teach not their own use; but that is a wisdom without them, and above them, won by observation. Read not to contradict and confute; nor to believe and take for granted; nor to find talk and discourse but to weigh and consider.

(a) According to the author, why should one study? (2 marks)
(b) Why does the author not recommend too much of studies? (2 marks)
(c) According to the author, how can studies be perfected? (2 marks)
(d) Which kind of human beings denounce studies? (2 marks)
(e) According to the author, why should one read? (2 marks)
4.explanation: Suggested answers: (a) Studies serve for delight, ornament and ability. (b) Too much time in study is sloth; using studies chiefly for ornament is affectation; judging only by study rules is the humour of a scholar. (c) Experience perfects studies. (d) Crafty men condemn studies. (e) Read to weigh and consider, not merely to contradict, accept without question, or make conversation.

24.explanation: “She writes a lot of books” uses the simple present for a habitual action and is fully grammatical, so option (b) “writes” is the best single printed answer. The official final key is multi-valued (“B&D”): both “writes” (habitual present) and “has written” (present perfect of experience) are accepted. Option (b) is recorded as the primary derived answer and the key’s acceptance of D is noted.

1.q: Write an essay choosing one topic: (a) Sairang Rail Station: A Catalyst for Infrastructure Development in Mizoram; (b) Mental Health and Work Environment; (c) Strengthening Good Governance through Official Statistics; or (d) The Digital Generation: How Technology Is Changing Childhood and Youth. (20 marks)
1.explanation: Choose one topic. Suggested approach: state a clear thesis, develop three or four relevant points with examples, organise the essay into an introduction, coherent body paragraphs and conclusion, and use accurate grammar. For topic (a), discuss connectivity, trade, tourism and regional development; for (b), workplace causes, effects and supports; for (c), reliable data, transparency and evidence-led decisions; for (d), learning, communication, wellbeing, privacy and responsible use.

2.q:
Write a précis of the following passage (10 marks):
Self-reliance is the pilgrim’s best staff, the worker’s best tool. It is the master key that unlocks all the difficulties of life. “Help yourself and Heaven will help you” is a maxim that receives daily confirmation. He who begins with crutches will generally end with crutches. Help from within always strengthens, but help from without invariably weakens the recipients. The habit of depending upon others should be vigorously resisted, since it tends to weaken the intellectual faculties and paralyse the judgement. The struggle against adverse circumstances has, on the contrary, a strengthening effect, like that of the pure mountain air on an enfeebled frame.

This is a lesson which is not taught in academic institutions nowadays. The vice of the modern system of education is that it lays down too many royal roads to knowledge. The difficulties, which formerly compelled the student to think and labour for himself are now removed. The race of thorough and complete scholars is dying out. Our young men are equipped to such an extent with manuals that explain everything and guides that go everywhere, that they find no occasion for thought. Why take any trouble at all when so many are willing to relieve you of it?
2.explanation: Sample précis (title: “The Value of Self-Reliance”): Self-reliance strengthens judgement and character. Depending constantly on others weakens independent thought, while facing difficulties develops intellectual ability. Education should therefore encourage students to think and work for themselves instead of relying entirely on ready-made guides. A good précis should be concise, use the writer’s main ideas and be expressed in the student’s own words.

3.q: According to the passage, why did people worship the forces of nature? (2 marks)
3.explanation: They were awed by the violent and powerful aspects of nature and felt overwhelmed by natural forces such as fire, the sun, rivers, rocks, trees and snakes.

4.q: Why does the passage say that science emerged as a “saviour of mankind”? (2 marks)
4.explanation: Religious authorities had monopolised spiritual knowledge and suppressed liberal or sceptical ideas, punishing thinkers. Science offered a path out of those intellectual chains and began to gain ground.

7.q: Give an antonym of “non-contradictory.” (2 marks)
7.explanation: A suitable antonym is “contradictory” or “inconsistent.” No answer options are printed for this short-answer item.

12.q: Give a synonym for “dazzled/impressed.” (2 marks)
12.explanation: Suitable synonyms include “awed,” “astonished” or “amazed.” No answer options are printed for this short-answer item.

13.q: Make sentences with any five pairs to show the difference in meaning: (a) Emerge/Immerse; (b) Pair/Pare; (c) Teem/Team; (d) Antique/Antic; (e) Compliment/Complement; (f) Hail/Hale; (g) Wave/Waive; (h) Proscribe/Prescribe. (5×2=10 marks)
13.explanation: Sample sentences: emerge—The sun emerged from the clouds; immerse—Immerse the cloth in water. pair—The pair arrived together; pare—Pare the apple. teem—The pond teems with fish; team—Our team won. antique—She bought an antique vase; antic—The clown’s antic made us laugh. compliment—He gave her a compliment; complement—The sauce complements the dish. hail—They hailed a taxi; hale—The hale veteran walked briskly. wave—She gave a friendly wave; waive—The bank agreed to waive the fee. proscribe—The law proscribes bribery; prescribe—The doctor will prescribe medicine.

14.q: Supply one-word substitutes for any ten: (a) incapable of making errors; (b) fluent and clear in speech; (c) one who hates war and loves peace; (d) a remedy for all ills; (e) exactly as spoken or written; (f) a connoisseur of food; (g) an imaginary name assumed by an author; (h) medicine given to counteract poison; (i) one who lives in solitude; (j) an examination of living tissue; (k) an official pardon; (l) a flower fastened in a circle. (10×2=20 marks)
14.explanation: Suggested answers: (a) infallible; (b) eloquent; (c) pacifist; (d) panacea; (e) verbatim; (f) gourmet/epicure; (g) pseudonym; (h) antidote; (i) recluse; (j) biopsy; (k) pardon/amnesty; (l) wreath.

15.q: Supply synonyms for any five: (a) Concur; (b) Overbearing; (c) Mitigate; (d) Prodigy; (e) Vagrant; (f) Brittle; (g) Disdain. (5×2=10 marks)
15.explanation: Suggested synonyms: concur—agree; overbearing—domineering; mitigate—alleviate; prodigy—genius; vagrant—wandering; brittle—fragile; disdain—contempt.

16.q: Supply antonyms for any five: (a) Moderate; (b) Jubilant; (c) Eccentric; (d) Nepotism; (e) Transient; (f) Spurious; (g) Abound. (5×2=10 marks)
16.explanation: Suggested antonyms: moderate—extreme; jubilant—despondent; eccentric—conventional; nepotism—impartiality; transient—permanent; spurious—genuine; abound—lack.

17.q: Make sentences with any five idioms/phrases to show their meaning: (a) Hold water; (b) Bird’s-eye view; (c) Apple-pie order; (d) To miss the bus; (e) A small fry; (f) Gordian knot; (g) Damp squib. (5×2=10 marks)
17.explanation: Sample uses: Her explanation does not hold water. From the hill we had a bird’s-eye view of the town. The files were arranged in apple-pie order. He missed the bus by arriving late. The manager treated no employee as a small fry. The mediator cut through the Gordian knot. The much-advertised event was a damp squib.

18.q: Change the voice: (a) The chef is cooking a special dish. (b) How did you open the door? (c) Tea shall not be taken by me today. (d) By whom were you insulted? (e) Mistakes were made. (5×2=10 marks)
18.explanation: Possible answers: (a) A special dish is being cooked by the chef. (b) How was the door opened? (c) I shall not take tea today. (d) Who insulted you? (e) Someone made mistakes. Passive sentences without an expressed agent may allow more than one natural active subject.

19.q: Complete the question tags: (a) Let us go, ___? (b) He isn’t very happy with it, ___? (c) Mind your business, ___? (d) Keep your mouth shut, ___? (e) Don’t break the glass, ___? (5 × 2 = 10 marks)
19.explanation: Suggested tags: (a) shall we? (b) is he? (c) will you? (d) will you? (e) will you? Commands commonly take “will you?” as the tag.

20.q: Rewrite as directed: (a) How long have you ___ him? (use “know”); (b) The sun was shining. We went for a walk. (make compound); (c) Having finished his work, he went home. (make complex); (d) You have to pay or you cannot leave this place. (make simple); (e) She said, “You see, you cannot meet the principal.” (indirect speech); (f) Portia exclaimed with sorrow that she was ruined. (direct speech); (g) Waste not, want not. (begin with “if”); (h) I do not know her nature any better than you. (use positive degree); (i) His prompt reply will able us to take timely action. (correct/improve); (j) Shall we ever forget these happy days? (rewrite using “never”). (10 × 2 = 20 marks)
20.explanation: Possible answers: (a) How long have you known him? (b) The sun was shining, so we went for a walk. (c) After he had finished his work, he went home. (d) You cannot leave this place without paying. (e) She said that I could not meet the principal. (f) Portia exclaimed, “Alas! I am ruined!” (g) If you do not waste, you will not want. (h) I know her nature no better than you do. (i) His prompt reply will enable us to take timely action. (j) We shall never forget these happy days.

opts.a: The Government is controlling the quota
opts.c: It is used extensively in construction

10.q: Which statement is false according to the passage?

opts.a: White cement is a controlled product
opts.b: The price rise is not caused by a production problem
opts.c: The price rise would upset the cement-tile market

10.explanation: The passage says cement was decontrolled, so saying white cement is a controlled product is false (A).

11.q: What crisis are cement-tile manufacturers facing, according to the passage?

opts.a: White cement is priced very low
opts.b: White cement prices are very high

12.q: Which word has the same meaning as “idle” as used in the passage?
12.explanation: In the passage 'idle capacity' means unused or surplus capacity, i.e. excess capacity. (D) Excess is the closest contextual match; 'lazy' describes a person, not capacity.

13.q: Which statement is correct according to the passage?

opts.a: White cement is not used to manufacture paint
opts.b: White cement is a minor part of tile manufacturing
opts.c: White cement is very important for tile manufacturing
opts.d: White cement is used only to make paint

opts.c: Use of white cement in other areas should be reduced
opts.d: Competition among cement-paint and tile manufacturers should be reduced

15.q: The profits will be equally divided ____ the two partners.

16.q: His chances are ____ than mine.

17.q: A horse is ____ like an elephant.
17.explanation: “A horse is not like an elephant” is the grammatical sentence (A).

18.q: I injured my knee four years ago, but I have been feeling pain in it ____.

23.explanation: The standard construction is “detrimental to,” so C is correct.

24.q: The robbers not only injured the landlord but also decamped ____ the booty.
24.explanation: “Decamp with” means leave with something, so D is correct.

25.q: “The old lady goes for a walk in the morning.” The verb form expresses:

26.q: “Unless you pay, you will be refused admission.” This expresses:
26.explanation: The conditional warns of a consequence if payment is not made; C is the intended answer.

27.q: “If I were you, I would not care for such a man.” This expresses:
27.explanation: The speaker recommends what the listener should do, so the sentence expresses advice (C).

28.q: “May you live long!” expresses:
28.explanation: “May you live long!” is an optative expression of a wish (D).

29.q: The manager said to his assistant, “Let the customers in.” This is an expression of:

opts.d: Both an order and a suggestion

29.explanation: In this context, the manager instructs the assistant to admit the customers; it is an order (B).

30.q: “She will be waiting for me when I reach her home.” The verb phrase is in the:
30.explanation: “Will be waiting” is the future progressive construction (B).

31.q: The verdict of the Judges that he is guilty has been challenged. Identify the sentence type.
31.explanation: “That he is guilty” is a subordinate noun clause in apposition to “verdict”; the sentence has a main clause and a subordinate clause, so it is complex (C).

32.q: He denied to have sold spurious drugs to the customers. Identify the sentence type.
32.explanation: The sentence contains one independent clause; “to have sold spurious drugs” is an infinitive phrase, not a finite subordinate clause. It is simple (B).

33.q: Morning walk is a good exercise, therefore everybody should walk. Identify the sentence type.
33.explanation: The sentence joins two independent clauses: “Morning walk is a good exercise” and “everybody should walk.” It is compound (A).

34.q: Everyone wonders how she completed this work. Identify the sentence type.
34.explanation: “How she completed this work” is a subordinate noun clause completing “wonders”; the sentence is complex (C).

35.q: Although they were tired, they worked late into the night. Identify the sentence type.
35.explanation: “Although they were tired” is a dependent adverb clause, so the sentence is complex (C).

36.q: You permit me and I shall leave the room. Identify the sentence type.
36.explanation: The sentence has two independent clauses joined by “and,” so it is compound (A).

37.q: **Rich as he is**, he is not happy. Identify the clause type of the underlined words.
37.explanation: “Rich as he is” is a concessive subordinate adverb clause (C).

38.q: I do not know **whom she is teaching**. Identify the clause type of the underlined words.
38.explanation: “Whom she is teaching” is the object of “know,” so it is a noun clause (A).

39.q: He told me **what his father told him**. Identify the clause type of the underlined words.
39.explanation: “What his father told him” is the content of what he told me and functions as a noun clause (B).

40.q: I shall go to the place **where my friend lives**. Identify the clause type of the underlined words.
40.explanation: 'Where my friend lives' modifies the noun 'place', so it functions as an adjective (relative) clause; the paper's intended answer is (B) Adjective clause.

41.q: **He could not utter a single word to his son** who, when he arrived, was in a dejected mood. Identify the clause type of the underlined words.
41.explanation: The underlined words form the main independent clause; they are the principal clause (C).

42.q: **Since my brother came**, he has been teaching. Identify the clause type of the underlined words.
42.explanation: “Since my brother came” gives the time of the teaching and is a subordinate adverb clause (B).

43.q: The prisoner was released on ____ for good behaviour.
43.explanation: Parole is conditional release from prison, commonly granted for good behaviour (C).

44.q: The brilliant students will be ____ scholarships.
44.explanation: The standard collocation is “awarded scholarships” (B).

45.q: The salt spray has gradually ____ the bridge.
45.explanation: Salt spray gradually wears away a structure, so “eroded” is the best fit (A).

46.q: On seeing the police approach, the miscreants ____.
46.explanation: “Took to their heels” means ran away, which fits the context (C).

47.q: If a speech is full of pompous words, it is ____.
47.explanation: Speech full of pompous, inflated words is described as grandiloquent. (D) Grandiloquent is the precise term, with 'bombastic' a near-synonym.

48.q: Because of the bitter experiences of the past, he ____ everywhere.
48.explanation: “Smell a rat” means suspect something wrong, matching the context (D).

49.q: He is very ____ on meeting foreigners and befriending them.
49.explanation: The idiom is “keen on” doing something, so D is correct.

50.q: We do not know what ____ him to commit this crime.
50.explanation: “What prompted him” means what induced or caused him to act; C is the best fit.

1.q: Section A (20 marks): Write an essay of no more than 300 words on any one topic: (a) Social media and its impact on society; (b) Role and significance of NGOs in Mizoram; (c) Crime against women in India.
1.explanation: Choose one topic and stay within 300 words. State a clear central idea, develop it with relevant examples and organise the response into an introduction, connected body paragraphs and a conclusion. For (a), consider benefits, risks and responsible use; for (b), discuss community development, advocacy and accountability in Mizoram; for (c), discuss forms and causes of violence, its effects, prevention and access to justice without blaming victims.

2.q:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows. In every field of life—be it sports, academics, music, or business—the discussion of talent versus hard work often arises. Some people believe that natural talent is the primary reason for success, while others argue that hard work plays a far more significant role. Talent refers to the natural ability that one is born with. For example, a person may have a natural talent for singing or mathematics. Such individuals often learn things faster and perform better at an early stage. However, relying solely on talent without consistent effort can be a mistake. History is full of examples where talented individuals did not achieve great heights because they lacked dedication and discipline. On the contrary, many people with average ability have excelled through determination, constant practice, and hard work. One such example is Thomas Alva Edison, who had limited formal education but became one of the greatest inventors due to his perseverance. Hard work not only improves skills but also builds character. It teaches discipline, time management, and patience. While talent can give an initial advantage, it is hard work that sustains long-term success. Moreover, hard-working individuals tend to be more adaptable and better prepared to face challenges, making them valuable assets in both personal and professional life. Employers and organizations increasingly value employees who show commitment, persistence, and a willingness to learn. In today’s competitive world, talent alone is no longer enough. The combination of effort, attitude, and continuous learning often outweighs pure natural ability. In conclusion, while talent may open doors, it is hard work that keeps them open.
(a) According to the passage, what is talent? (1)
(b) Why did some talented people not succeed? (1)
(c) What do modern employers value most in employees? (1)
(d) Which is not a benefit of hard work? (i) Builds character; (ii) Improves appearance; (iii) Teaches time management; (iv) Helps face challenges. (1)
(e) Why is relying solely on talent a mistake? (2)
(f) What are the benefits of hard work? (2)
(g) How does Thomas Alva Edison’s example support hard work over talent? (2)
(h) Talent opens doors, but hard work keeps them open. Elaborate. (2)
(i) How does hard work relate to adaptability in personal and professional life? (2)
(j) Do you think discipline alone can lead to success, or is talent also necessary? (2)
(k) Find passage words similar to (i) innate and (ii) surpassed. (1+1=2)
(l) Find passage words opposite to (i) failure and (ii) rigid. (1+1=2)
2.explanation: Passage answers: (a) Talent is an inborn natural ability. (b) They lacked dedication and discipline. (c) Commitment, persistence and willingness to learn. (d) Improves appearance, option ii. (e) Talent without consistent effort may not sustain success. (f) Better skills and character, discipline, time management and patience. (g) Edison’s perseverance overcame limited formal schooling. (h) Talent can create an initial opportunity, but work sustains it. (i) Practice prepares people to adjust and meet challenges. (j) Give a reasoned view using the passage; it supports effort and continuous learning while recognising talent’s initial advantage. (k) innate—natural; surpassed—outweighs is the nearest passage expression, though its tense differs. (l) failure—success; rigid—adaptable.

3.q: Read the following passage carefully and write a precis in about one third of its length. Suggest a suitable title.(10) In our modern society, academic degrees are often seen as the primary measure of a person’s intelligence and capability. From an early age, students are encouraged to pursue higher education, with the promise that a degree will ensure a successful and prosperous future. Employers frequently prioritize candidates with formal qualifications, and society places high esteem on those who have studied at reputed institutions. However, this growing dependence on degrees has led to the undervaluation of something equally, if not more, important—common sense. Common sense refers to the ability to make sound judgments based on practical knowledge and everyday experiences. It is not something that can be taught in textbooks or classrooms. While education equips individuals with theoretical knowledge, it does not always prepare them for real-life challenges. Many highly educated people struggle when faced with everyday problems that require practical thinking, while others with little formal education navigate these situations with ease. For instance, a person might hold an advanced degree in business management but still lack the basic understanding of dealing with people or handling unforeseen circumstances. Moreover, common sense often leads to innovation and creativity. Some of the most successful entrepreneurs and leaders in history did not possess extensive formal education but excelled because of their sharp instincts, decision-making ability, and practical wisdom. This is not to undermine the value of education—it is undoubtedly important—but it should be complemented by real-world understanding. In conclusion, while a degree might open doors, common sense is what helps individuals make the most of those opportunities. Success in life is not solely determined by academic achievements, but also by one’s ability to think clearly, make wise choices, and respond effectively to challenges. Both education and common sense are valuable, but relying solely on degrees can be misleading.
3.explanation: Suggested title: Education and Practical Wisdom. In about one third of the passage’s length, explain society’s emphasis on degrees, the distinct value of practical judgement, the limitations of purely theoretical education, and the need to combine education with common sense. Do not imply that formal education is worthless.

1.q: Which state became the first in India to achieve 100% literacy as of May 2025?

11.explanation: The Golden Crescent and Golden Triangle are names for major opium-producing and trafficking regions in Asia.

15.explanation: Samudragupta is known as the “Napoleon of India,” a label associated with his extensive military campaigns.

65.explanation: The official MPSC final answer key (Paper-II) marks (B) Amazon Rainforest, a globally recognized biodiversity hotspot.

66.explanation: An invasive species is introduced outside its native range and causes ecological, economic, or other harm. Mere migration or rarity does not make a species invasive.

67.explanation: Climate describes long-term patterns and averages of weather in a region; weather refers to shorter-term conditions.

68.explanation: India’s National AQI is calculated from eight pollutants: PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, NH3 and lead. Carbon dioxide is not on that list. The stem was edited from “gases” to “pollutants,” because particulate matter is not a gas.

70.explanation: India’s national programme identifies 18 Biosphere Reserves. The printed “Biodiversity Reserves” is not the name of this notified programme, so the stem is corrected to “Biosphere Reserves.”

71.explanation: Pyramids of numbers and biomass can be inverted in some ecosystems. The pyramid of energy is always upright because energy is lost between trophic levels.

72.explanation: The Ramsar-listed Pala Wetland site covers about 18.5 km² (1,850 hectares). This is the designated wetland site area, not only the open-water area of Pala Lake; “recently designated” was removed because the listing dates to 2021.

73.explanation: Combustion of coal, oil and natural gas releases large amounts of carbon dioxide and is the largest human source among these choices.

74.explanation: Sulfur dioxide is emitted directly from sources such as fuel combustion, so it is a primary pollutant. Ozone and PAN form in the atmosphere as secondary pollutants.

75.explanation: Gravity attracts us toward Earth and keeps us on its surface.

76.explanation: O-negative red blood cells lack A, B and Rh(D) antigens, so they are used as the universal red-cell donor type in emergencies. Compatibility still depends on the clinical context.

77.explanation: The liver is the body’s largest gland.

78.explanation: A concave reflector behind the bulb directs the headlamp beam forward.

82.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movement and helps maintain balance and posture.

88.explanation: Tawlhlohpuan is associated with courage and victory; traditional accounts connect it with a warrior’s bravery.

91.explanation: The Chawngchilhi folktale centres on a snake with which Chawngchilhi falls in love.

99.explanation: Fathang was a rice or paddy tribute paid by households to the village chief.

100.explanation: R. A. Lorrain is credited with developing the Mara alphabet. F. W. Savidge also produced earlier Mara-language work, which makes “credited with developing” more precise than claiming he had no role in written Mara.

hfw-2026-p2.evidence: Group B technical common examination under Health & Family Welfare, January 2026, Paper-II (General Studies). Q1–20 were checked against the printed cover and pages 1–2; all numbered stems, option wording and four-option sets were compared with the scan. The cover specifies 100 one-mark questions and two hours, with no negative-marking instruction. Nineteen answers have independently derived explanations. Q14 is held because “within India’s boundary” can refer to India’s claimed boundary (K2) or territory under Indian administration (Kangchenjunga), and the stem does not specify which. Questions 21–40 were checked against printed pages 2–4; stems, numbering and all options were verified. All twenty have independently derived explanations. Q24 is clarified to distinguish Presidential assent (15 June) from the Act coming into force (12 October). Questions 41–60 were checked against printed pages 4–6; all stems and option sets were checked for completeness and legibility. All twenty have independently derived explanations. Q44’s expected season was checked against the Lai District Government’s festival description; Q52’s award was checked against the Urban Mobility India award record. Questions 61–80 were checked against printed pages 6–7; all stems, numbering and options were checked. All twenty have independently derived explanations. Q64 spelling and Q68 longitude typography/options were corrected for readability; Q75 was clarified because the phrase “first defined” was historically imprecise, while the Brundtland Report contains the widely used definition. Questions 81–100 were checked against printed pages 7–8; all stems, numbering and four-option sets were verified against the scan. Twenty answers have independently derived explanations. Q95 is keyed to the mismatched Duhmanga–Thanghniangi pair after checking Mizo Studies (Mizoram University) and the Tribal Research Institute folklore catalogue; Q90 uses “genotype” as the closest available choice, though “genome” is technically more exact for a complete genetic complement. Q81 was verified against the Ramsar site record and Q86 against the Tamil Nadu State Wetlands Authority.

1.q:
Read the Internet-addiction passage on the printed page. Write a précis in about one third of its length and suggest a suitable title. (10 marks)

In the United States, they have opened their first rehabilitation centre for Internet Addicts. De-addiction camps in China were in the news recently for the death of a teenager because of the brutal methods used to cure ‘Internet Addiction’ (IA). Our country must seriously think about such centres that help de-addict compulsive Internet-users, both young and old. IA for now is a catch-all term that not only stands for addiction to specific activities such as gambling or gaming, but also refers to longer hours devoted to the computer network at the expense of other activities. Though, the Internet is only a medium of communication and information transmission and retrieval (like the printed book or television), ‘addiction’ is being used in this case with concern because of a fundamental dialectic: ‘quantity becomes quality.’ A whole new world is just a click away with the Internet. It is a medium just like books and television, but the amount of interaction it makes possible with others, sometimes replacing the need for real world interaction, makes it vastly different. Educators, neuroscientists and those others having public health concerns in all developing and developed countries have woken upto this reality. According to expert neuropsychiatric opinion, IA is somewhere between Obsessive Compulsive Disorder and the addiction due to substance abuse. Substance abuse led addiction focuses on gratification, which this form of attachment provides, though there is no chemical ingestion. At the same time, the behavioural modifications are similar to those with Obsessive Compulsive Disorder. It is almost like the ‘rush’ gamblers get out of a purely gratification-oriented repetitive action.
1.explanation: Sample title: “The Internet and Addiction.” Sample précis: Internet addiction includes compulsive gaming or gambling and excessive online activity that displaces other parts of life. Although the Internet is a medium like books or television, its constant availability and interactive nature can make overuse harmful. Experts view the condition as sharing features with obsessive-compulsive disorder and substance addiction: it offers gratification without chemical intake, while producing similar behavioural changes. Society should develop humane ways to help users regain balance. A précis should retain these central ideas, use original concise wording and be about one third as long as the passage.

2.q:
Read the passage about Sweden’s Parliamentary Ombudsman. Answer all parts. I. Find words from the passage similar in meaning to: (a) with too much or undesired enthusiasm (b) rebuke somebody officially (c) obliged to obey (d) strongly (e) dislike based on fear or false information. (5×1=5) II. Answer: (a) Why did Sweden introduce the institution of Ombudsman? (1) (b) How is an Ombudsman chosen in Sweden? (1) (c) How does the Ombudsman investigate and act upon citizens’ complaints? (2) (d) How can the public find out about the Ombudsman’s work? (2) (e) What did the Chief of Police deny? (2) (f) How did the Ombudsman decide the case? (2)

Passage: The Scandinavian countries are much admired all over the world for their enlightened social policies. Sweden has evolved an excellent system for protecting the individual citizen from high-handed or incompetent public officers. The system has worked so well that it has been adopted in other countries like Denmark, Norway, Finland and New Zealand. Even countries with large populations are now seriously considering imitating the Swedes. The Swedes were the first to recognize that Public officials like civil servants, police officers, health inspectors or tax collectors can make mistakes or act overzealously in the belief that they are serving the public. As long ago as 1809, the Swedish Parliament introduced a scheme to safeguard the interests of the individual. A parliamentary committee representing all political parties appoints a person who is suitably qualified to investigate private grievances against the State. The official title of the person is Justice Ombudsman but Swedes commonly refer to him as the J.O. or just Ombudsman. The Ombudsman is not subject to political pressure. He investigates complaints, large and small, that come to him from all levels of society. As complaints must be made in writing, the Ombudsman receives an average of 1200 letters a year. He has eight lawyer assistants to help him, and he examines every single letter in detail. There is nothing secretive about the Ombudsman’s work, for his correspondence is open to public inspection. If a citizen’s complaint is justified, the Ombudsman will act on his behalf. The action he takes varies according to the nature of the complaint. He may gently reprimand an official or even suggest to parliament that a law be altered. The following case is a typical example of the Ombudsman’s work. A foreigner living in a Swedish village wrote to the Ombudsman, complaining that he had been ill- treated by the police, simply because he was a foreigner. The Ombudsman immediately wrote to the Chief of Police in the district, asking him to send a record of the case. There was nothing in the record to show that the foreigner’s complaint was justified and the Chief of Police stoutly denied the accusation. It was impossible for the Ombudsman to take action on the complaint, but when he received a similar complaint from another foreigner in the same village, he immediately sent one of his lawyers to investigate. The lawyer ascertained that a policeman had indeed dealt roughly with foreigners on several occasions. The fact that the policeman was prejudiced against foreigners could not be recorded in the official files. It was possible only for the Ombudsman to find this out by sending one of his representatives to check the facts on the spot. The policeman in question was severely reprimanded and was informed that if any further complaints were received against him, he would be prosecuted. The Ombudsman’s prompt action in the manner at once put an end to an unpleasant practice which might have gone on unnoticed.
2.explanation: I. (a) overzealously (b) reprimand (c) subject to (d) stoutly (e) prejudiced. II. (a) To protect citizens from high-handed or incompetent public officials. (b) A parliamentary committee representing all parties appoints a suitably qualified person. (c) He examines written complaints, requests records and may send a lawyer to investigate; if justified, he reprimands the official or recommends a change in law. (d) His correspondence is open to public inspection. (e) The Chief denied that the policeman had ill-treated the foreigner. (f) After another similar complaint, the Ombudsman sent a lawyer who confirmed the policeman’s repeated rough treatment; the policeman was reprimanded and warned of prosecution if it recurred.

The extracted Q1–8 had been merged into one corrupt record; Q1–8 were reconstructed from printed page 2, and Q9–24 were compared against printed pages 2–3. 47.explanation: In standard English 'although' introduces a subordinate clause and must not be paired with the coordinating conjunction 'but' (or 'yet') in the same sentence, so options A, B and D are defective. Option C, 'Although he was tired, he continued working', is the clean, grammatically correct sentence. 1.q:
Write a précis of the following passage in about one third of its length. Suggest a suitable title. (10 marks)

In the modern world, money is often seen as the ultimate measure of success and security. People devote their lives to earning more, believing that wealth guarantees happiness, comfort, and respect. While money undoubtedly plays a crucial role in meeting basic needs and providing opportunities, it is not the most important thing in life. Beyond a certain point, the pursuit of money can lead to stress, unhealthy competition, and strained relationships.

True happiness and fulfillment often come from sources that money cannot buy—such as love, health, peace of mind, and meaningful human connections. A wealthy person without friends or health is not truly rich. Moreover, ethical values, compassion, and a sense of purpose add far more to a person’s life than material possessions. The world has seen countless examples of individuals who, despite limited means, lived content and impactful lives.

Money should be viewed as a tool, not a goal. It is meant to support life, not define it. A balanced approach—where one earns enough for comfort but does not let money dictate all decisions—is essential for a wholesome life. As societies evolve, there is a growing realization that quality of life cannot be measured by income alone, but by the richness of experiences, relationships, and personal growth.
1.explanation: Model précis (about one third length): “Money is necessary for security and opportunity, but beyond basic comfort, its pursuit can bring stress and damage relationships. Happiness depends more on health, love, peace, ethical values, purpose and meaningful connections than on wealth. Money should support life rather than define it; a balanced life is measured by experiences, relationships and personal growth.” Suitable title: “Money and True Happiness.”

3.q:
Read the passage and answer all ten questions below. (Questions (a)–(e) on page 2 carry 1 mark each; questions (f)–(j) on page 3 carry 2 marks each.)

Exercise is essential for maintaining a healthy lifestyle. It helps improve cardiovascular health, strengthens muscles, and boosts the immune system. Regular physical activity also reduces the risk of chronic diseases such as heart disease, diabetes, and obesity. Additionally, exercise plays a crucial role in mental well-being by reducing stress, anxiety, and depression.

There are different types of exercises, including aerobic exercises like running and swimming, strength training like weightlifting, and flexibility exercises such as yoga and stretching. A combination of these exercises ensures overall fitness and health. Experts recommend at least 30 minutes of moderate exercise per day to maintain good health.

The lack of physical activity has become a major concern, especially with modern lifestyles that involve sitting for long hours. Many people spend excessive time on screens, leading to a sedentary lifestyle. This can result in weight gain, muscle weakness, and poor cardiovascular health. To stay active, individuals can take small steps such as walking instead of driving, using stairs instead of elevators, and participating in sports or outdoor activities.

Governments and health organizations promote exercise through awareness campaigns, fitness programs, and policies that encourage active lifestyles. Schools also play a key role by including physical education in their curriculum. Exercise is not just about fitness—it is a way to enhance the quality of life and increase life expectancy.

(a) ______ exercise includes activities like running and swimming.
(b) A sedentary lifestyle can lead to ______ gain.
(c) Give a synonym of “guarantee” (the question says “second paragraph”).
(d) Give an antonym of “diminish” (the question says “fourth paragraph”).
(e) Give one way in which a school can promote physical activity.
(f) What flexibility exercises are mentioned in the passage?
(g) Why is exercise important for overall health?
(h) How does exercise contribute to mental well-being?
(i) How can individuals include more physical activity in their daily routine?
(j) What role do governments and health organizations play in promoting exercise?
3.explanation: Answer guide: (a) aerobic; (b) weight; (c) ensure(s), which appears in the second paragraph and means to make certain; (d) increase, the antonym of “diminish” used in the fourth paragraph. (e) include physical education in the curriculum; (f) yoga and stretching; (g) it improves cardiovascular health, strengthens muscles, boosts immunity and lowers chronic-disease risk; (h) it reduces stress, anxiety and depression; (i) walk instead of driving, use stairs, or take part in sports/outdoor activities; (j) run awareness campaigns and fitness programs and adopt policies encouraging active lifestyles.

The worst days of any summer are the rainy ones. We spend all year looking forward to nice weather and long, hot days. All of winter, with its dreary gray days and bitter cold, we dream of those endless days at the beach, laying on the sand and soaking in the bright and burning sun. Mostly, the days run together, bleeding into each other so that they no longer seem like separate entities and instead feel like continuations of the same long day. Everything seems monotonous and dull, and an ennui or listlessness kicks in. Such a mindset makes you cheer for anything new or different. I spend the winter dreaming of summer and the summer dreaming of winter. When summer comes, I complain about how hot it is. Power foods are foods that provide rich levels of nutrients like fibre, potassium, and minerals. With people becoming increasingly health-conscious today, a lot of fitness trainers encourage their clients to include these foods in their daily diet to increase muscle development. There are various ways of incorporating power foods in your daily diet. Of course, the key to enjoying power foods is proper preparation of these foods, the use of season-fresh foods, and identifying your choice of flavour among power foods.

Some of the recommended power-food combinations are those prepared in our kitchens on a regular basis. Take, for instance, the combination of chickpeas and onions. This combination is a powerful source of iron, which is required by the body to transport oxygen to its various parts. Iron deficiency can lead to anaemia, fatigue, brain fog, and tiredness. A study by the Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry says that sulphur compounds in onion and garlic help in the absorption of iron and zinc from chickpeas. The combination is a hit with teenagers who need to be diligent about getting iron in their diet. A quick way to prepare this power food is to make a chickpea salad with chopped onions, chaat masala, and cilantro.

Another favourite combination with power-food takers is yoghurt and bananas. This makes for a perfect snack after a rough game of football. Exercising burns glucose and thus lowers blood sugar. Yoghurt is packed with proteins that help preserve muscle mass, and bananas are packed with carbohydrates that help in refuelling energy and preventing muscle soreness. A quick and easy recipe with bananas is a banana smoothie topped with cool yoghurt.

Among beverages, green tea is the best source of catechins that are effective in halting oxidative damage to cells. According to researchers at Purdue University, adding a dash of lemon juice to green tea makes the catechins more easily absorbed by the body. So, the next time you have friends over, serve them rounds of iced green tea with mint and lemon juice.

81.q: Based on the passage, Hooker lost the Battle of Chancellorsville mostly because of his —
81.direction:
Directions: Read the passage and answer Questions 81–85 based on it.

The Battle of Chancellorsville, one of the most famous battles of the Civil War, took place in Virginia in the spring of 1863. For months, the two armies had been staked out on opposite banks of a narrow river. The Confederate troops were led by perhaps the most revered military tactician in American history, General Robert E. Lee. The Union soldiers were led by “Fighting” Joe Hooker. In appearance, personality, and lifestyle, these men were nearly perfect opposites. Lee, an older man in poor health with a gray beard, had a somber, measured demeanor. Hooker was a blond, strapping young man whose vanity over his appearance was but one aspect of his egotism. Whereas Lee was devout and principled, Hooker was known for his rollicking enjoyment of both women and whiskey.

Despite the fact that the Confederacy had won the last four major battles and the Union soldiers were famished, exhausted, and demoralized, Hooker proclaimed, “My plans are perfect. And when I start to carry them out, may God have mercy on Bobby Lee, for I shall have none.” Why, aside from a propensity for narcissism, was Hooker so confident? Hooker had used spies, analysts, and even hot-air balloons to compile a vast amount of intelligence about Lee’s army. He had discerned, for example, that Lee had only 61,000 men to Hooker’s own 134,000. Buoyed by his superior numbers, Hooker covertly moved 70,000 of his men fifteen miles up and across the river, and then ordered them to sneak back down to position themselves behind Lee’s army. In effect, Hooker had cut off the Confederate soldiers in front and behind. They were trapped. Satisfied with his advantage, Hooker became convinced that Lee’s only option was to retreat to Richmond, thus assuring a Union victory.

Yet Lee, despite his disadvantages of both numbers and position, did not retreat. Instead, he moved his troops into position to attack. Union soldiers who tried to warn Hooker that Lee was on the offensive were dismissed as cowards. Having become convinced that Lee had no choice but to retreat, Hooker began to ignore reality. When Lee’s army attacked the Union soldiers at 5:00 p.m., they were eating supper, completely unprepared for battle. They abandoned their rifles and fled as Lee’s troops came shrieking out of the brush, bayonets drawn. Against all odds, Lee won the Battle of Chancellorsville, and Hooker’s forces withdrew in defeat.

opts.b: support the idea that Lee was more virtuous and therefore a better commander.
opts.c: suggest that Hooker would not have been outwitted if he had been more devout.
opts.d: imply that the men differed in their approaches to nearly everything, including battle.

Directions: Read the passage and answer Questions 86–90 based on it.

Persuasion is the art of convincing someone to agree with your point of view. According to the ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle, there are three basic tools of persuasion: ethos, pathos, and logos.

Ethos is a speaker’s way of convincing the audience that she is a credible source. An audience will consider a speaker credible if she seems trustworthy, reliable, and sincere. This can be done in many ways. For example, a speaker can develop ethos by explaining how much experience or education she has in the field. After all, you would be more likely to listen to advice about how to take care of your teeth from a dentist than a firefighter. A speaker can also create ethos by convincing the audience that she is a good person who has their best interests at heart. If an audience cannot trust you, you will not be able to persuade them.

Pathos is a speaker’s way of connecting with an audience’s emotions. For example, a speaker who is trying to convince an audience to vote for him might say that he alone can save the country from a terrible war. These words are intended to fill the audience with fear, thus making them want to vote for him. Similarly, a charity organization that helps animals might show an audience pictures of injured dogs and cats. These images are intended to fill the viewers with pity. If the audience feels bad for the animals, they will be more likely to donate money.

Logos is the use of facts, information, statistics, or other evidence to make your argument more convincing. An audience will be more likely to believe you if you have data to back up your claims. For example, a commercial for soap might tell you that laboratory tests have shown that its soap kills all 7,000,000 of the bacteria living on your hands right now. This piece of information might make you more likely to buy that brand of soap. Presenting this evidence is much more convincing than simply saying “our soap is the best!” Use of logos can also increase a speaker’s ethos: the more facts a speaker includes in an argument, the more likely you are to think that the speaker is educated and trustworthy.

Although ethos, pathos, and logos all have their strengths, they are often most effective when used together. Indeed, most speakers use a combination of ethos, pathos, and logos to persuade their audiences. The next time you listen to a speech, watch a commercial, or listen to a friend try to convince you to lend him some money, be on the lookout for these ancient Greek tools of persuasion.

If I don’t get these new shoes, everyone at school is going to laugh at me. I will be so embarrassed that I will want to die.” What form of persuasion is Amy using here?

opts.d: A combination of ethos, pathos, and logos

92.direction:
Directions: Read the passage and answer Questions 91–100 based on it.

Power foods are foods that provide rich levels of nutrients like fibre, potassium, and minerals. With people becoming increasingly health-conscious today, a lot of fitness trainers encourage their clients to include these foods in their daily diet to increase muscle development. There are various ways of incorporating power foods in your daily diet. Of course, the key to enjoying power foods is proper preparation of these foods, the use of season-fresh foods, and identifying your choice of flavour among power foods.

Some of the recommended power-food combinations are those prepared in our kitchens on a regular basis. Take, for instance, the combination of chickpeas and onions. This combination is a powerful source of iron, which is required by the body to transport oxygen to its various parts. Iron deficiency can lead to anaemia, fatigue, brain fog, and tiredness. A study by the Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry says that sulphur compounds in onion and garlic help in the absorption of iron and zinc from chickpeas. The combination is a hit with teenagers who need to be diligent about getting iron in their diet. A quick way to prepare this power food is to make a chickpea salad with chopped onions, chaat masala, and cilantro.

Another favourite combination with power-food takers is yoghurt and bananas. This makes for a perfect snack after a rough game of football. Exercising burns glucose and thus lowers blood sugar. Yoghurt is packed with proteins that help preserve muscle mass, and bananas are packed with carbohydrates that help in refuelling energy and preventing muscle soreness. A quick and easy recipe with bananas is a banana smoothie topped with cool yoghurt.

Among beverages, green tea is the best source of catechins that are effective in halting oxidative damage to cells. According to researchers at Purdue University, adding a dash of lemon juice to green tea makes the catechins more easily absorbed by the body. So, the next time you have friends over, serve them rounds of iced green tea with mint and lemon juice.

Power foods are foods that provide rich levels of nutrients like fibre, potassium, and minerals. With people becoming increasingly health-conscious today, a lot of fitness trainers encourage their clients to include these foods in their daily diet to increase muscle development. There are various ways of incorporating power foods in your daily diet. Of course, the key to enjoying power foods is proper preparation of these foods, the use of season-fresh foods, and identifying your choice of flavour among power foods.

Some of the recommended power-food combinations are those prepared in our kitchens on a regular basis. Take, for instance, the combination of chickpeas and onions. This combination is a powerful source of iron, which is required by the body to transport oxygen to its various parts. Iron deficiency can lead to anaemia, fatigue, brain fog, and tiredness. A study by the Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry says that sulphur compounds in onion and garlic help in the absorption of iron and zinc from chickpeas. The combination is a hit with teenagers who need to be diligent about getting iron in their diet. A quick way to prepare this power food is to make a chickpea salad with chopped onions, chaat masala, and cilantro.

Another favourite combination with power-food takers is yoghurt and bananas. This makes for a perfect snack after a rough game of football. Exercising burns glucose and thus lowers blood sugar. Yoghurt is packed with proteins that help preserve muscle mass, and bananas are packed with carbohydrates that help in refuelling energy and preventing muscle soreness. A quick and easy recipe with bananas is a banana smoothie topped with cool yoghurt.

Among beverages, green tea is the best source of catechins that are effective in halting oxidative damage to cells. According to researchers at Purdue University, adding a dash of lemon juice to green tea makes the catechins more easily absorbed by the body. So, the next time you have friends over, serve them rounds of iced green tea with mint and lemon juice.

1.q:
Write a précis of the following passage and give a suitable title.

Gardening is one of the oldest and most rewarding human activities. Long before the rise of
   modern cities and industries, people cultivated plants not only for food but also for beauty and peace
   of mind. In today’s fast-paced world, gardening remains a quiet yet powerful way to reconnect with
   nature and oneself. It teaches patience, care, and respect for life. Watching a seed sprout, grow, and
   bloom is a reminder that growth cannot be hurried and that every living thing requires time and
   attention to flourish. Beyond personal satisfaction, gardening plays a vital role in environmental balance.
   Gardens act as miniature ecosystems that support a variety of life—bees, butterflies, birds, and
   countless microorganisms. In urban areas, gardens help reduce air pollution, provide shade, and
   lower temperatures. They also improve soil quality and contribute to water conservation when managed
   responsibly. Even a few pots on a balcony can make a difference by absorbing carbon dioxide and
   releasing oxygen. Thus, gardening, in its simplest form, becomes a small act of environmental activism.
   Moreover, gardening promotes mental and physical well-being. Studies have shown that spending
   time with plants reduces stress, lowers blood pressure, and improves concentration. Digging, planting,
   and weeding are gentle forms of exercise that keep the body active and flexible. The sense of purpose
   that comes from nurturing life can lift one’s mood and help overcome feelings of anxiety or loneliness.
   For many, gardens become personal sanctuaries—a place to reflect, create, and find joy in the smallest
   details of life. Gardening also encourages sustainability and self-reliance. Growing one’s own fruits,
   vegetables, and herbs reduces dependence on commercially grown products, which often involves
   heavy use of chemicals and long-distance transportation. A home garden promotes healthier eating
   habits and teaches respect for the effort involved in producing food. Community gardens, in particular,
   bring people together. They transform unused spaces into areas of cooperation, sharing, and friendship.
   People from different backgrounds come together to work on a common project, bridging gaps and
   strengthening community ties. However, modern lifestyles and urbanization have made gardening
   more challenging. Limited space, lack of time, and disconnection from nature discourage people from
   taking up this rewarding activity. Yet, with creativity and determination, gardening can be adapted to
   modern life. Vertical gardens, hydroponics, and rooftop gardens are examples of innovative solutions
   that bring greenery into compact spaces. Schools and workplaces can also introduce gardening
   programs to foster awareness of sustainability and environmental care among young people. In the
   end, gardening is more than a hobby; it is a way of life. It teaches responsibility, gratitude, and
   balance. A gardener learns that every season has its rhythm, every plant its need, and every effort its
   reward. As cities grow and technology advances, the humble act of tending to a plant reminds us that
   we are still part of nature, not separate from it. To garden is to nurture life, and in doing so, to nurture
   the gardener’s own soul.

Read the given passage carefully and answer the questions that follow. Your answers must be based on the passage only. On a radiant Saturday morning, Bara Bazar, the commercial heart of Aizawl, pulsated with characteristic vitality. The air was an intricate blend of aroma- smoked meat, roasted corn, and freshly harvested vegetables- interwoven with the hum of animated bargaining. Stalls overflowed with vivid textiles, fruits, and handicrafts, while the rhythm of footsteps and voices formed the living music of the marketplace. Amidst this dynamic scene moved an elderly woman, a vendor from a nearby village. She bore a woven bamboo basket laden with oranges and bananas, the product of her modest livelihood. Her steps were deliberate yet weary from the long descent from her hillside home. As she approached the Dawrpui junction steps, the uneven pavement caused her to stumble slightly, sending her basket tumbling to the ground. The fruits scattered chaotically, rolling between stalls and down the slope, drawing the attention of nearby onlookers. For a brief interlude, the bustling crowd seemed suspended in hesitation. Some individuals watched with detached curiosity, while others appeared momentarily uncertain of how to intervene. It was then that a group of college students, observing the incident, instinctively hurried forward. Demonstrating commendable civic empathy, they gathered the fallen fruits with meticulous care, brushing away dust and restoring them to the basket. One student extended a steadying hand to the woman, while another insisted on carrying her burden up the remaining flight of steps. The woman’s countenance, once clouded with distress, softened into an expression of profound gratitude. In a trembling yet affectionate voice, she uttered, “Thank you, may God bless you.” The sincerity of her words evoked a quiet sense of reverence among the bystanders. Nearby vendors nodded approvingly, some offering the young helpers roasted corn and tea as tokens of appreciation. For a few fleeting moments, the frenetic rhythm of the marketplace seemed to dissolve into a shared stillness—a recognition of genuine human solidarity. The scene, though simple, encapsulated a deeper moral truth: that kindness persists even amidst the noise of modern urban life. For the onlookers, the episode served as a subtle yet powerful reminder of communal compassion and ethical responsibility, virtues deeply embedded within Mizo culture. Amid the hurried exchanges and commercial bustle of Bara Bazar, that small gesture of humanity shone like a quiet beacon—affirming that benevolence, however ordinary, continues to bind society together in its most authentic form.

Answer these questions based only on the passage: (a) What caused the elderly woman’s mishap? (b) How did the students show civic empathy? (c) How did the woman express gratitude? 1.q:
Read the given passage carefully and write a précis of it, giving an appropriate title. (10)
It is very easy to acquire bad habits, such as eating too many sweets or too much food, or
drinking too much fluid of any kind, or smoking. The more we do a thing, the more we tend to like
doing it; and, if we do not continue to do it, we feel unhappy. This is called the force of habit, and the
force of habit should be fought against.

Things which may be very good when only done from time to time, tend to become very
harmful when done too often and too much. This applies even to such good things as work or rest.
Some people form a bad habit of working too much, and others of idling too much. The wise man
always remembers that this is true about himself, and checks any bad habits. He says to himself, “I
am now becoming idle,” or “I like too many sweets,” or “I smoke too much” and then adds, “I will
get myself out of this habit at once”.

One of the most widely spread of bad habits is the use of tobacco. Tobacco is now smoked or
chewed by men, often by women, and even by children almost all over the world. It was brought into
Europe from America, from Sir Walter Raleigh, four centuries ago and has thence spread everywhere.
I very much doubt whether there is any good in the habit, even when tobacco is not used to excess;
and it is extremely difficult to get rid of the habit when once it has been formed.

Alcohol is taken in almost all cool and cold climates, and to a very much less extent in hot ones.
Thus, itis taken by people who live in the Himalaya Mountains, but not nearly by those who live in the
plains of India. Alcohol is not necessary in anyway to anybody. Millions of people are beginning to do
without it entirely; and once the United States of America have passed laws which forbid its manufacture
or sale throughout the length and breadth of their vast country. In India, it is not required by the
people at all, and should be avoided by them altogether. The regular use of alcohol, even in small
quantities, tends to cause mischief in many ways to various organs of the body. It affects the liver, it
weakens the mental power, and lessens the general energy of the body.
1.explanation: Write a concise précis that captures the passage’s central argument: repeated habits can become harmful; people should recognize and resist such habits, especially tobacco and alcohol use. Give an appropriate title, use your own words, and omit illustrations and repetition.

Read the passage and answer on its basis only.

I stopped to let the car cool off and to study the map. I had expected to be near my objective
by now, but everything still seemed alien to me. I was only five when my father had taken me abroad,
and that was eighteen years ago, when my mother had died after a tragic accident, he did not quickly
recover from the shock and loneliness. Everything around him was full of her presence, continually
reopening the wound. So he decided to emigrate. In the new country, he became absorbed in making
a new life for the two of us, so that he gradually ceased to grieve. He did not marry again and I was
brought up without a woman’s care; but I lacked nothing, for he was both father and mother to me.
He always meant to go back one day. but not to stay. His roots and mine had become too firmly
embedded in the new land. But he wanted to see the old folk again and to visit my mother’s grave. He
became mortally ill a few months before we had planned to go and, when he knew that he was dying,
he made me promise to go on my own.

I hired a car the day after landing and bought a comprehensive book of maps, which I found
most helpful on the cross-country journey, but which I did not think I should need on the last stage. It
was not that | actually remembered anything at all. But my father had described over and over again
what we should see at every milestone, after leaving the nearest town, so that I was positive I should
recognize it as familiar territory. Well, I had been wrong, for I was now lost.

I looked at the map and then at the speedometer. I had come ten miles since leaving the town,
and at this point, according to my father, I should be looking at farms and cottages in a valley, with the
spire of the church of our village showing in the far distance. I could see no farms, no cottages and
church spire—only a lake. I decided that I must have taken a wrong turning somewhere. So I drove
back to the town and began to retrace the route, taking frequent glances at the map. I landed up at
the same corner. The curious thing was that the lake was not marked in the map. I felt as if I had
stumbled into a nightmare country, as you sometimes do in dreams. And, as in a nightmare, there was
nobody in sight to help me. Fortunately for me, as I was wondering what to do next, there appeared
on the horizon a man on horseback, riding in my direction. I waited till he came near, then I asked him
the way to our old village. He said that there was now no village. I thought he must have misunderstood
me, so I repeated its name. This time he pointed to the lake. The village no longer existed because it
had been submerged, and all the valley too. The lake was not a natural one, but a man-made reservoir.

(a) Why did the author’s father emigrate? (b) Why did the author not feel the absence of his mother after her death? (c) Why did his father want to return to the old village? (d) Why did the author return to his birthplace? (e) Why did he think he would not need a map for the final part of the journey? (f) Why could he not locate the old village? (g) Give words from the passage meaning: (i) a frightening or unpleasant dream; (ii) to go under the surface of water; (iii) a vehicle instrument showing speed.

            The classical realist theory of international relations has long dominated both academic institutions

     classical realists ask, what are the causes of war and what are the conditions of peace? The members
     of the classical realist school mainly attribute war and conflict to what is termed the security dilemma.
     In the absence of any prevailing global authority, each nation is required to address its own security
     needs. However, each nation’s quest for security—through military build ups, alliances, or territorial
     defences— necessarily unsettles other nations. These nations react to feelings of insecurity by engaging
     in their own aggressive actions, which leads other nations to react similarly, perpetuating the cycle. It
     is important to note that for realists, unlike idealists or liberal internationalists, international conflict is
     a necessary consequence of the structural anarchy that nations find themselves in. Whereas other
     schools may see international conflict as the result of evil dictators, historical chance, flawed socio-


   political systems, or ignorance of world affairs, classical realists see war as the logical result of a
   system that by its nature lacks a true central authority. Hand in hand with this view of conflict as an
   inevitable condition of the global power structure is the realists’ view of the nation as a unitary actor.
   Because classical realists see international relations as a continuing struggle for dominance, the nation
   cannot be viewed as a collection of individuals with disparate wants, goals, and ideologies. The
   realist view requires the formulation of a national interest, which in its simplest terms refers to the
   nation’s ability to survive, maintain its security, and achieve some level of power relative to its
   competitors. Realism is not without its critics, many of whom challenge the premise that war is the
   natural condition of international relations or that there can be a truly national interest. However, the
   realist school of international relations continues to shape foreign policy because of the successes it
   has had in describing real world interactions between nations.
   Questions :
    (a) The formation of a national interest serves what function in the classical realist theory of war
        and peace, based on the passage?                                                             (5)
    (b) What argument would members of the classical realist school would be least likely to support?(5)
    (c) What will best support the classical realist theory of international conflict?               (5)
    (d) What is the underlying principle of classic realism?                                         (5)
3.explanation: Answer from the passage: (a) A national interest treats the nation as a unitary actor pursuing survival, security and relative power. (b) Realists would reject the claim that conflict is merely accidental or can be eliminated by removing a few bad leaders. (c) Reciprocal military build-ups and defensive alliances that increase other states’ insecurity illustrate the security dilemma. (d) The central concern is the causes of war and conditions of peace within a system lacking a prevailing global authority.

            The cinema is an outstanding wonder of this modern age. Apart from the great pleasure it gives
     us as a means of entertainment, it is in many ways an education itself, and no regular patron of the
     cinema can be called illiterate. The cinema is also a very valuable asset to educationists. The film
     companies, from time to time, produce historical pictures and their pictures are of great importance
