     of animals, insects, fishes, germs and numerous other branches of scientific life. We can see the
     hatching of the egg of fish and their gradual development into large fishes; we can watch the unceasing
     activity of many kinds of germs and their effect on water, milk or blood. We can watch the opening
     and closing of flowers and leaves and the growth of grass and weeds. All these actions and movements

     cause of education.

1.q:
Write a précis of the following passage in about one third of its length : (10)

The great advantage of early rising is the good start it gives us in our day’s work. The early riser
has done a large amount of hard work before other men have gotten out of bed. In the early morning
the mind is fresh, and there are few sounds or other distractions, so that work done at that time is
generally well done. In many cases the early riser also finds time to take some exercise in the fresh
morning air, and this exercise supplies him with a fund of energy that will last until the evening. By
beginning so early, he knows that he has plenty of time to do thoroughly all the works he can be
expected to do, and is not tempted to hurry over any part of it. All his works being finished in good
time, he has a long interval of rest in the evening before the timely hour when he goes to bed. He gets
to sleep several hours before midnight, at the time when sleep is most refreshing and after a sound
night’s rest, rises early next morning in good health and spirits for the labours of a new day.

It is very plain that such a life as this is far more conducive to health than that of the man who
shortens his waking hours by rising late, and so can afford in the course of the day little leisure for
necessary rest. Any one who lies in bed late, must, if he wishes to do a full day’s work, go on working
to a correspondingly late hour, and deny himself the hour or two of evening exercise that he ought to
take for the benefit of his health. But, in spite of all his efforts, he will probably produce as good
results as the early riser, because he misses the best working hours of the day.

It may be objected to this that some find the perfect quiet of midnight by far the best time for
working. This is no doubt true in certain cases. Several great thinkers have found by experience that
their intellect is clearest, and they can write best, when they burn the midnight oil. But even in such
cases the practice of working late at night cannot be commended. Few men, if any, can exert the full
power of their intellect at the time when nature prescribes sleep, without ruining their health thereby;
and of course the injury done to the health must in the long run have a bad effect on the quality of the

work done.
1.explanation: Suggested title: Advantages of Early Rising. Write about one third of the original length. Retain the author’s central claims about a fresh mind, productive mornings, exercise, adequate time, evening rest and the long-term health cost of late-night work. Note that the printed sentence “he will probably produce as good results … because he misses the best working hours” is internally inconsistent; summarise the overall argument without adding a new claim.

Computers are capable of doing extremely complicated work in all branches of learning. They
can solve the most complex mathematical problems or put a thousand unrelated data in order. These
machines can be put to varied uses. For instance, they can provide information on the best way to
prevent traffic accidents. They work accurately and at high speed. They save research workers’
years of hard work.

This whole process, by which machines can be used to work for us, has been called ‘automation’.
In future, automation may enable human beings to enjoy more leisure than they do today. The coming

of automation is bound to have important social consequences,


Some years ago, an expert on automation, Sir Leon Bagrit, pointed out that it was a mistake to
believe that these machines could think. There is no possibility that human beings will be controlled
by machines. Though computers are capable of learning from their mistakes and improving on their
performances, they need detailed instructions from human beings to be able to operate. They can
never lead independent lives or ‘rule the world’ by taking decisions of their own.

Sir Leon said that, in future, computers would be developed which would be small enough to
be carried in one’s pocket. Ordinary people would then be able to use them to obtain valuable
information. Computers could be plugged into a wireless network and could be used like radios. For
instance, people going on a holiday could be informed about weather conditions. Car drivers can be
given an alternative route when there is a traffic jam. It will also be possible to make tiny translating
machines. This will enable people who do not share a common language to talk to each other without
any difficulty or to read foreign publications.

It is impossible to assess the importance of a machine of this sort, for many international
misunderstandings are caused simply due to our failure to understand one another. Computers will
also be used in ordinary public hospitals. By providing a machine with a patient’s systems, a doctor
will be able to diagnose the nature of his illness. Similarly, machines could be used to keep a check on
a patient’s health record and bring it up to date. Doctors will, therefore, have immediate access to
great many facts which will help them in their work. Book-keepers and Accountants too, could be
relieved of dull clerical work. For, the tedious task of compiling and checking lists of figures could be
done entirely by machines. Computers are the most efficient servant that man has ever had, and there
is no limit to the way they can be used to improve our lives.


Questions:
(a) What is the limitation of computers? (1)
(b) In the opinion of the writer, which benefits can be derived from automation? (2)
(c) In paragraph 1, the writer says “computers can provide information in the best way”. Explain in context. (2)
(d) Is it True or False that Automation would not give any leisure time to human beings? (1)
(e) In the context of the passage, the synonym of “monotonous” is _____. (1)
(f) List two areas where computers can be used effectively. (2)
(g) How can the benefits suggested in paragraph 3 be best described? (2)
(h) Why is it fair to say that computers will help a lot even in ordinary public hospitals? (2)
(i) The writer believes that automation will bring social _____. (1)
(j) Give a suitable title for the passage. (1)
2.explanation: Answer from the passage: (a) They require detailed human instructions and cannot take independent decisions. (b) Faster accurate work and more leisure. (c) They process data to identify ways of preventing traffic accidents. (d) False. (e) Tedious / dull. (f) Hospitals and accountancy, or traffic management and translation. (g) Pocket-sized networked information and translation tools; the paragraph reference is loose, so identify the relevant benefits explicitly. (h) They aid diagnosis and keep accessible, updated patient records. (i) consequences. (j) Suggested title: Computers and Automation. The passage’s historical view of computer capabilities is reproduced for comprehension, not asserted as a current technical assessment.

1.q:
Write a précis of the following passage and supply a suitable title. (10)

The primary advantage of waking up early is that it offers a head start on the day’s tasks, The
early riser would have had finished a significant amount of work before others have gotten out of bed.
The mind is clear in the early morning, because there are few sounds or distractions, so work done at
this point is often excellent. In several instances, early risers find time for physical activity in the fresh
morning air, which provides them with energy to last until the evening. By beginning early, they ensure
that they are given sufficient time to carry out all of the work that is expected of them and are not
compelled to rush through any of it. With all of their jobs completed on time, they get a considerable
period of leisure in the evening before going to bed at the appropriate hour. They retire to bed many
hours before midnight, when sleep is most pleasant, and wakes up early the next morning in good
health and enthusiasm to face the challenges of the day.

It is obvious that such a life is far more beneficial to health than that of the person who shortens
his/her waking hours by rising late, leaving little time during the day for vital rest. Anyone who falls
asleep late must, if they desire to complete a full day’s work, work until a suitably late hour and deny
themselves the hour or two of evening exercise that they should get for their health. Despite their best
efforts, they will most likely fail to achieve the same outcomes as the early riser because they have
missed the most productive hours of the day.

It may be disputed that some people find midnight to be the absolute finest time to work. This
is undeniably true in certain situations. However, even in such instances, working late at night is not
recommended. Few people, if any, can exercise the full strength of their brain at a time when nature
prescribes sleep without jeopardising their health; and, of course, the health damage must have a
negative impact on the quality of the work done in the long term.
1.explanation: Suggested title: The Benefits of Early Rising. Summarise the author’s argument that early rising allows productive work, exercise and evening rest, while habitual late work risks health and performance. Use your own words and retain the qualification that some people find midnight productive.

3.q:
Read the passage carefully. Then choose the correct answer.

Natural disasters have become frequent occurrences in the world today. Now and again, news
of serious flooding, earthquakes and tsunamis stun us. Things are destroyed and countless lives are
lost too. When incidences such as these take place, people wonder as to the cause(s) of these
events. Could these disasters be prevented in the first place? In the race to become a developed
country and a modern society, human beings have made tremendous changes to the environment.
When humans start meddling with Mother Nature, the effects can be disastrous at times. Rapid
development has caused many problems to humans and animals alike.

Everywhere we go, it is apparent that many areas are being developed to pave the way for
modernisation. New roads, industrial areas, townships and housing areas are replacing jungles and
hilly areas. In the process, countless trees have been cut down, jungles cleared and hilly areas flattened.
It has been scientifically proven that when trees are gone, water can no longer
be contained underground. The roots of trees that act as natural defences to hold water in the ground
are no longer there to do their job. As a result, rainwater flows straight out to sea in a much shorter
time, causing frequent flash floods to places that have never faced such problems before.

Development comes at a very high price. Animals and human lives are in danger. Many land
areas are turned into housing areas, including scenic hills. Houses and apartments, some of them
very highly priced, have been built on these scenic but unsafe hills. Without careful study, and over
time, the unstable ground condition often caves in causing landslides that kill many people.

The clearing of land for all kinds of reasons has also led to the extinction of many wildlife
species. In the first place, land development causes the destruction of many animal habitats. Animals
now have to compete with humans for space and food. To survive, these animals are forced to move
deeper into the jungles. Their sources of food have become scarce, thus threatening their survival.
Smaller spaces and less food have led to the extinction of some species. Fifteen endangered animals
and six critically endangered animals in Malaysia have been identified. The Malayan Tapir, the Malayan
Tiger and the Asian elephant are three large mammal species that are on the endangered species list.
Among the critically endangered ones are the black shrew, the Malayan water shrew, the Malayan
roundleaf bat and the Sumatran rhinoceros.

It is obvious that many animals have been sacrificed in the name of development and
modernisation. Indiscriminate human activities have led to the destruction of irreplaceable and priceless
lives. There are laws to curb people from messing with our forests, polluting and doing things that can
harm our environment. There are also laws to punish those who do so, but the laws do not seem to
serve their purpose. It is the responsibility of each and every individual to preserve our fragile Earth.
If we keep destroying it, we will soon lose all that we have.

your answer. (2)
(e) Who is responsible for the preservation of nature around us? (2)

2.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow:                                      (8×2=16)
                  Many of us believe that ‘small’ means ‘insignificant’. We believe that small actions and
       choices do not have much impact on our lives. We think that it is only the big things, the big actions
       and the big decisions that really count. But when you look at all the lives of all great people, you will
       see that they built their character through small decisions, small choices and small actions that they
       performed every day. They transformed their lives through step-by-step or day-by-day approach.
       They nurtured and nourished their good habits and chipped away their bad habits, one by one. It was
       their small day-to-day decisions that added up to make tremendous difference in the long run. Indeed,
       in matters of personal growth and character building, there is no such thing as an overnight success.
                 Growth always occurs through a sequential series of stages. There is an organic process to
       growth. When we look at children growing up, we can see this process at work: the child first learns
       to crawl, then to stand and walk and then finally to run. The same is true in the natural world. The soil
       must first be tilled and then the seed must be sown. Next, it must be nurtured with enough water and
       sunlight and only then will it grow into trees laden with ripe fruits.
                 Gandhi understood this organic process and used this universal law of nature to his benefit.
       Gandhi grew in small ways, in his day-to-day affairs. He did not wake up one day and find himself to
       be the ‘Mahatma’. In fact, there was nothing much in his early life that showed signs of greatness. But
       from his mid-twenties onwards, he deliberately and consistently attempted to change himself, reformed
       himself and grew in some small ways every day. Day by day, hour by hour, he risked failure,
       experimented and learnt from mistakes. In small as well as large situations, he took up the responsibility
       rather than avoiding it.
                This is a common factor in the lives of all great people: they exercise their freedoms and
       choices in small ways that make great impact on their lives and their environment. Each of their small
       decisions and actions, add up to have a profound impact in the long run. By understanding this
       principle, we can move forward, with confidence, in the direction of our dreams. Often when our
       ideal goal, looks too far from us, we become easily discouraged, disheartened and pessimistic.


     However, when we choose to grow in small ways, by taking small steps one at a time, our achievement
     becomes easy.


  (i) The main idea in the first paragraph is that :
       (a) big things, big actions and big decisions make a person great.
       (b) small actions and decisions are important in one’s life.
       (c) overnight success is possible for all of us.
       (d) personal changes are not important.
 (ii) What does the writer mean by saying ‘chipped away at their bad habits’?
       (a) Steadily gave up bad habits.                (b) Slowly produced bad habits.
       (c) Gradually criticized bad habits.            (d) Did not like bad habits.
 (iii) What is done by great people to transform their lives?
        (a) They approach life on a day-to-day basis.      (b) They build character in small ways.
        (c) They believe in performing every day.          (d) All of these.
 (iv) How can we grow in small ways?
       (a) By getting disheartened.                        (b) By dreaming little.
       (c) By taking small steps one at a time.            (d) None of these.
 (v) How did Gandhiji become ‘Mahatma’?
      (a) By risking failures.                             (b) By learning from mistakes.
      (c) By taking up responsibilities.                   (d) All of the above.
 (vi) What according to the author is the universal law of nature?
       (a) Everything takes time to grow.                  (b) Nothing can change in a day.
       (c) Both (a) & (b)                                  (d) Neither (a) nor (b)
(vii) Pick out the word/phrase which is similar in meaning to ‘purposely’
       (a) intentionally                                  (b) deliberately
       (c) in small ways                                  (d) consistently
(viii) Pick the right option in which the word ‘Principle’ has been used in the same way as in Para 4 of the
       passage
        (a) He was a man of principle and good to his word.
        (b) The ambassador refused on principle to agree to the terms of the accord.
        (c) By one count, rice is the principle source of calories for about half the planet.
        (d) Wilson constructed various forms of electric wave detector depending on this same principle.
                                                   -3-
2.explanation: Passage answers: (i) B—small actions and decisions matter; (ii) A—steadily gave up bad habits; (iii) D—all of these; (iv) C—small steps; (v) D—all of the above. (vi) A expresses gradual growth; C is probably intended but B’s absolute “nothing can change in a day” is too sweeping. (vii) Deliberately is the word used in the passage; intentionally is also synonymous with purposely, so without a passage-word restriction A and B overlap. (viii) D uses principle as an underlying rule rather than a moral conviction. C misprints principal as principle. These are guidance for the conventional response sheet, not machine-scored subquestions.

2.q: Write a précis of the following passage in about 1/3 of its original length, giving it suitable title.(10) Trees give shade for the benefit of others, and while they themselves must stand directly in the sun and endure the scorching heat of the day, they continue to produce the fruit by which others profit. They do not hoard their gifts, nor do they complain of the weather. The character of good and noble men is exactly like that of these trees. We must ask ourselves: what is the use of this perishable body, which is destined to decay, if no use of it is made for the lasting benefit of mankind? A life lived only for the self is a life wasted. Consider the natural world and the lessons it yields. Take sandalwood- the more it is rubbed against a hard surface, the more of its sweet scent does it yield to the air. Consider the sugarcane— the more it is peeled, crushed, and cut into small pieces, the more delicious juice does it produce for the thirsty. Look at gold—the more it is burnt in the crucible of the forge, the more brightly and purely does it shine. The men who are truly noble at heart do not lose these divine qualities even in the process of losing their very lives. To them, the external world is secondary. What does it matter whether common men praise them or not? What difference does it make whether great riches abide with them or whether they live in poverty? What does it signify whether they die at this very moment or whether their lives are prolonged for many years? Happen what may, those who tread in the right path of righteousness will not set foot in any other, for their integrity is absolute. Life itself is unprofitable and hollow to a man who does not live for the service of others. To live for the mere sake of living one’s own life is to live the base life of dogs and cows, driven only by instinct. Those who lay down their lives, even for the sake of a friend, or even for the sake of a complete stranger, will assuredly dwell forever in a world of eternal bliss.

4.q:
Read the following passage and answer the question given below: Many people believe that science and religion are contrary to each other. But this notion is wrong. As a matter of fact, both are complementary to each other. The aim of both these institutions is to explain different aspects of life, universe and human existence. There is no doubt that the methods of science and religion are different. The method of science is observation, experimentation and experience. Science takes its recourse to progressive march towards perfection; the rules of religion are faith, intuition and spoken word of the enlightened; in general, while science is inclined towards reason and rationality, spiritualism is the essence of religion. In earlier times when man appeared on earth, he was over-awed at the sight of violent and powerful aspects of nature. In certain cases, the usefulness of different natural objects of nature overwhelmed man. Thus began the worship of forces of nature-fire, the sun, the rivers, the rocks, the trees, the snakes, etc. The holy scriptures were written by those who had developed harmony between external nature and their inner self. Their object was to ennoble, elevate and liberate the human spirit and mind. But the priestly class took upon itself the monopoly of scriptural knowledge and interpretation to its own advantage. Thus the entire human race was in chains. Truth was flouted and progressive, liberal and truthful ideas or ideas expressing doubt and skepticism were suppressed and their holders punished. It was in these trying circumstances, the science emerged as a saviour of mankind. But its path was not smooth and safe. The scientists and free thinkers were tortured. This was the fate of Copernicus, Galileo, Bruno and others. But by and by science gain ground.
(a) Why does man worship the force of nature? (2)
(b) Why does the passage say that science emerged as a saviour of mankind? (2)
(c) How does it distinguish science’s methods from religion’s? (2)
(d) What treatment did early scientists like Galileo and Bruno face, and why? (2)
(e) How does the author argue against science and religion being contrary? (2)
4.explanation: According to the passage: (a) Awe at powerful natural forces and appreciation of useful natural objects led to worship. (b) Science challenged suppression of truth and free inquiry. (c) Science uses observation, experimentation and experience; religion uses faith, intuition and teachings of the enlightened. (d) Early thinkers were tortured or persecuted for challenging established interpretations. (e) The author argues that both explain aspects of life and existence through different, complementary methods. These are comprehension answers representing the author’s claims.

1.q:
Write a precis of the passage given below: (10)

Culture is a forbidding word. I have to use it, knowing of none better to describe the various
beautiful and interesting objects which man has made in the past and handed down to us, and which
some of us are hoping to hand on. Many people despise them. They argue with force that cultural
stuff takes up a great deal of room and time, and better be scrapped.

Cultivated people are like drops in an ocean. They mix easily and genially with other drops, for
those exclusive days are over when cultivated people made only cultivated friends, and became
tongue-tied or terror-struck in the presence of anyone whose make-up was different from their own.
Culture, thank goodness, is no longer a social asset, it can no longer be employed either as a barrier
against the mob or as a ladder into the aristocracy.

All the same, we are a drop in the ocean. Few people share our enjoyment so far. Strictly
between ourselves, and keeping our limited circulation in mind, let us put our heads together and
consider for a moment our special problem, our special blessings, our special woes. No one needs to
listen to us who does not want to. We whisper in the corner of a world which is full of others’ noises,
and louder ones.

Come closer, our problem, as I see it, is what we have got worth passing on. What we have is

3.q:
Read the given passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

A majority taken collectively may be regarded as a being whose opinions and, most frequently,
whose interests are opposed to those of another being, which is styled a minority. If it is admitted that
a man possessing absolute power may misuse that power by wronging his adversaries, why should a
majority not be liable to the same reproach? Men are not apt to change their characters by
agglomeration; nor does their patience in the presence of obstacles increase with the consciousness
of their strength. For these reasons we should not willingly invest any group of our fellows with that

unlimited authority which we should refuse to any individual.



One social power must always predominate over others, but liberty is endangered when this
power is checked by no obstacles which may retard its course and force it to moderate its own
vehemence. Unlimited power is in itself a bad and dangerous thing, and no power on earth is so
worthy of honor for itself or of reverential obedience to the rights which it represents that we should
admit its uncontrolled and all-predominant authority. When the right and means of absolute command
are conferred on a people or a king, on an aristocracy or a democracy, a monarchy or a republic,
there has been implanted the germ of tyranny.

The main evil of the present democratic institutions of the United States does not arise, as is
often asserted in Europe, from their weakness, but from their overpowering strength; the excessive
liberty which reigns in that country is not so alarming as is the very inadequate security which exists
against tyranny.

When an individual or a party is wronged in the United States, to whom can he apply for
redress? If to the public opinion, public opinion constitutes the majority; if to the legislature, it represents
the majority and implicitly obeys its injunctions; if to the executive power, it is appointed by the
majority and remains a passive tool in its hands; the public troops consist of the majority under arms;
the jury is the majority invested with the right of hearing judicial cases, and in certain states even the
judges are elected by the majority. However iniquitous or absurd the evil complained about, no sure
barrier is established to defend against it.


Find the passage words matching: (a) autocracy [freedom/tyranny/liberty/anarchy]; (b) opponents [leaders/partners/adversaries/allies]; (c) blame [reproach/praise/reward/ignore]; (d) collection [dispersion/agglomeration/separation/scattering]; (e) nobility [aristocracy/democracy/oligarchy/monarchy]; (f) wicked [virtuous/justified/iniquitous/benign]. (6×1=6)
(g) What is the main theme of the passage? (3)
(h) What is the author’s main concern regarding unlimited power? (3)
(i) What is the author’s argument about individual liberty? (3)
3.explanation: Vocabulary answers: tyranny; adversaries; reproach; agglomeration; aristocracy; iniquitous. (g) The passage warns against unchecked majority power. (h) Unlimited authority can become tyranny whether held by one person or a group. (i) Liberty needs effective checks and avenues of redress against the dominant power. Answer according to the historical author’s argument, rather than treating it as a current assessment of US institutions.

1.direction: Direction (Question Nos. 1 - 10): Answer the following questions as directed:
1.q: In the sentence, “*The regional committee met* ***weekly*** *to review the mining lease applications,*” what part of speech is the word ‘weekly’?
1.explanation: ‘Weekly’ modifies the verb ‘met’ by telling how often the committee met, so it is an adverb.

2.direction: Direction (Question Nos. 1 - 10): Answer the following questions as directed:
2.q: In the sentence, “*We must find a* ***fast*** *solution to the slope stability issue before the monsoon begins,*” what part of speech is the word ‘fast’?
2.explanation: ‘Fast’ describes the noun ‘solution’, so it functions as an adjective.

3.direction: Direction (Question Nos. 1 - 10): Answer the following questions as directed:
3.q: In the sentence, “*The surveyor walked* ***past*** *the boundary pillar without noticing the structural damage,*” what part of speech is the word ‘past’?
3.explanation: ‘Past’ is followed by the noun phrase ‘the boundary pillar’, which makes it a preposition here.

4.direction: Direction (Question Nos. 1 - 10): Answer the following questions as directed:
4.q: In the sentence, “*The department decided to* ***house*** *the new core samples in the main laboratory,*” what part of speech is the word ‘house’?
4.explanation: ‘House’ means to provide a place for the samples. It is the main verb of the infinitive phrase ‘to house’.

5.direction: Direction (Question Nos. 1 - 10): Answer the following questions as directed:
5.q: In the sentence, “***Neither*** *the operator nor the safety engineer cleared the quarry site for blasting,*” what part of speech is the word ‘neither’?
5.explanation: ‘Neither’ is paired with ‘nor’ to join the two subjects, so it functions as a correlative conjunction.

6.q: In which of the following sentences is the word “iron” used as an adjective?

8.q: Read the sentence: “*The team completed the environmental audit fairly quickly.*” What does the adverb “fairly” modify?
8.explanation: ‘Fairly’ modifies the adverb ‘quickly’, indicating the degree to which the audit was completed quickly.

1.q:
Write a précis of the following passage. (14) Exploration and quarrying operations in the North-Eastern hill regions, particularly in states like Mizoram, encounter unique structural and environmental vulnerabilities that distinguish them from mining activities in mainland Indian plateaus. The combination of steep terrain, high-intensity monsoon rainfall, and young, seismically active geological formations creates a high-risk environment for standard extraction methods. Minor minerals, primarily sandstone and stone boulders used for regional infrastructure, are frequently extracted through small-scale, fragmented quarrying units.

Unfortunately, these units often lack the engineering capacity to manage high vertical faces, leading to frequent slope failures and landslides that endanger both labour and nearby settlements. Furthermore, the practice of stone crushing near highway corridors generates significant particulate matter, which degrades air quality and settles on surrounding vegetation, causing long-term agricultural distress.

To mitigate these localized hazards, mining administrative bodies must mandate systematic terracing and bench-formation protocols tailored specifically to steep slopes. It is no longer sufficient to regulate mineral revenue alone; the administration must actively oversee the hydrological impact of quarrying. Proper drainage networks must be constructed around lease areas to prevent rainwater accumulation from liquefying the soil overburden. Furthermore, the District Mineral Foundation (DMF) funds must be strategically utilized to rehabilitate abandoned quarry sites through targeted afforestation and loose-boulder check dams. Balancing the accelerating demand for construction aggregates with the ecological preservation of fragile hill slopes represents the defining administrative challenge for modern mining controllers in the region.

While Mizoram is not characterized by large-scale heavy metalliferous deposits like the iron or coal belts of central India, its unique inventory of non-metallic resources, including high-grade sandstone, shale, and potential clay deposits, forms the backbone of its localized industrial growth. The strategic position of the state, serving as a gateway for trans-national infrastructure projects like the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project, has exponentially escalated the domestic consumption of these structural minerals.

However, translating this resource wealth into equitable economic development requires a departure from ad-hoc extraction practices. The state’s mineral policy must prioritize structured resource appraisal over hasty extraction to ensure long-term availability. Unregulated quarrying not only causes revenue leakage through illegal transport networks but also prevents the state from commanding fair market value for its natural assets.

To rectify this, the modern mining administration must deploy digital monitoring tools, such as drone-based volumetric surveys and electronic transit passes, to plug leakage and accurately map the depletion rates of active stone quarries. Simultaneously, economic growth must not alienate local communities. Under the current mineral governance paradigms, sustainable development requires that a portion of the royalties collected be re-invested into local village councils for infrastructure and health initiatives. By transitioning from a primitive, revenue-only collection mindset to an asset-management approach, the state can secure its infrastructural self-reliance without bankrupting its environmental capital. The objective is to establish a system where mineral extraction funds long-term regional development rather than short-term private gain.

3.q:
Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow:
 The mining and processing of minerals provides us with the building blocks required to form much of the infrastructure needed to support modern societies. However, the process of mining remains intense and invasive, and operations often leave environmental impacts on the local surroundings as well as wider implications for the environmental health of the planet.

Mining and mineral processing operations often have high water footprints as many stages require the use of water. Examples include dust mitigation, removing soluble particles, sieving and separation processes, and in creating tailings dams for waste management. High water use in mining operations can lead to reduced access for local people to uncontaminated freshwater supplies and can result in a local area suffering from water stress. However, compared to other industries, mining has a relatively small water usage and often a large fraction of the water used is saline so it does not have much use in other industries or domestically.

Another issue related to environmental pollution caused by mining is that of leakages of mining tailings. Mining tailings are the materials left behind after the economically valuable fraction of material has been extracted. Modern mining programmes often aim to remove these harmful but valuable chemicals to reuse for further mineral separation. In addition to improving efficiency and cutting costs, this minimises the risk of environmental damage by reducing the toxicity of the tailings.

Overall, when considering the environmental ramifications of mining, it is important to weigh up the social and environmental damages caused by extracting the minerals against the benefits gained from the use of the final product. Mining of further resources is required to support the growing global population, but it should allow for the creation of green infrastructure and renewable energy generation. It is vital that governments and companies continue to innovate to create clean mining technologies with strict environmental regulations which will enable the mining industry to pave the way for a sustainable and hopeful future.

4.passage:
The mining and processing of minerals provides us with the building blocks required to form much of the infrastructure needed to support modern societies. However, the process of mining remains intense and invasive, and operations often leave environmental impacts on the local surroundings as well as wider implications for the environmental health of the planet.

Mining and mineral processing operations often have high water footprints as many stages require the use of water. Examples include dust mitigation, removing soluble particles, sieving and separation processes, and in creating tailings dams for waste management. High water use in mining operations can lead to reduced access for local people to uncontaminated freshwater supplies and can result in a local area suffering from water stress. However, compared to other industries, mining has a relatively small water usage and often a large fraction of the water used is saline so it does not have much use in other industries or domestically.

Another issue related to environmental pollution caused by mining is that of leakages of mining tailings. Mining tailings are the materials left behind after the economically valuable fraction of material has been extracted. Modern mining programmes often aim to remove these harmful but valuable chemicals to reuse for further mineral separation. In addition to improving efficiency and cutting costs, this minimises the risk of environmental damage by reducing the toxicity of the tailings.

Overall, when considering the environmental ramifications of mining, it is important to weigh up the social and environmental damages caused by extracting the minerals against the benefits gained from the use of the final product. Mining of further resources is required to support the growing global population, but it should allow for the creation of green infrastructure and renewable energy generation. It is vital that governments and companies continue to innovate to create clean mining technologies with strict environmental regulations which will enable the mining industry to pave the way for a sustainable and hopeful future.

21.explanation: The final key selects under, meaning below the table. The source supplies no picture or spatial context, so this is the keyed interpretation rather than a rule that a book must always be under a table.

22.explanation: Across describes movement from one side of the room to the other. The other choices do not give the intended complete spatial phrase here.

23.explanation: A picture attached to the surface of a wall is hanging on the wall. On expresses that surface relation.

24.explanation: For introduces a duration: for more than two hours. Since would instead introduce a starting point, but it is not one of the printed choices.

25.explanation: By plus a means of transport expresses how someone travelled: by train. No article is needed in this construction.

26.explanation: Into expresses movement from outside the river to inside it. Jumped into the river therefore describes entering the water.

27.explanation: Interested takes the preposition in before the activity: interested in dancing.

28.explanation: At the door identifies a position beside the doorway. The printed word wairing is a source typo; the preposition question is unaffected.

29.explanation: The idiom is afraid of something: afraid of the dark.

30.explanation: In is used with a year: born in 1960. On is normally used with a specific date or day; at with a particular time.

31.explanation: Eloquent means fluent and effective in expression. Praise for clarity and depth supports eloquent, whereas verbose means excessively wordy and ambiguous means unclear.

32.explanation: Scepticism means doubt. The contrast with later gained acceptance shows that the theory was initially doubted.

33.explanation: A forced smile is put on rather than spontaneous. It can hide disappointment, unlike a genuine or radiant smile.

34.explanation: Biased means unfairly favoring one side or group. Favoring only selected employees is evidence of bias; impartial, neutral and objective suggest fairness.

35.explanation: Insatiable means impossible to satisfy. Endless questions show curiosity that never seems satisfied.

36.explanation: Relentless efforts are persistent and sustained. This fits success through effort rather than luck; sporadic, casual and indifferent do not.

37.explanation: Flawed means defective or containing an error. An argument with defects can weaken a case; compelling and persuasive would strengthen it.

38.explanation: Insensitive remarks disregard other people’s feelings and can offend them. The other choices imply consideration or courtesy.

39.explanation: Keep one’s powder dry means remain prepared while waiting for the right moment to act. Here investors should conserve their resources and remain ready, rather than panic or spend immediately.

40.explanation: A sweeping statement makes a very broad generalization without accounting for individual cases. All politicians are corrupt generalizes about the whole group.

41.explanation: Come to the fore means become prominent or receive attention. Diversity and inclusion have become prominent workplace concerns.

42.explanation: Have a finger in the pie means be involved in an activity or affair, often with some influence over it.

43.explanation: The salt of the earth describes good, honest, dependable people. The phrase praises character, not merely sensitivity or leisure.

44.explanation: The sentence has the main clause I have no time and the subordinate relative clause that I can waste on idle talk. A main clause plus a subordinate clause makes it complex.

45.explanation: Not makes the statement negative. The sentence remains declarative in function, but Negative Sentence is the final key’s classification among the printed choices.

46.explanation: As rich as expresses comparison in the positive degree of the adjective rich; it does not use richer or richest. The final key calls this Positive Sentence. That printed label refers to the comparison pattern here.

47.explanation: Who was formerly your foe is a subordinate relative clause modifying her. The presence of that clause makes the sentence complex even though the main clause is a question.

48.explanation: The final key selects Assertive Sentence because the sentence makes a statement. My countrymen is a form of address and does not by itself turn the statement into a question or command. Affirmative describes its positive polarity, so the printed labels overlap.

49.explanation: The statement says that she enjoys an activity and contains no negation. It is affirmative; it is neither a command, a question nor an exclamation.

50.explanation: Finish your work on time gives a command or instruction with an understood subject you. That is an imperative sentence.

51.explanation: In a very soft voice tells how she spoke and modifies the verb spoke. The underlined prepositional phrase therefore functions as an adverb phrase.

52.explanation: Could have been told combines the modal could with auxiliary verbs have and been and the past participle told. Together they form a verb phrase.

53.explanation: Even though introduces a concession: he continued working despite complete exhaustion. Since would give a cause and as long as a condition, which do not express the intended contrast.

54.explanation: An embedded question uses statement order, where I was going, rather than the direct-question order where was I going. Was also matches the past reporting verb asked.

55.explanation: The standard first conditional uses present simple in the if-clause and will plus the base verb in the result: If you work hard, you will succeed.

56.explanation: When scarcely begins a clause, auxiliary-subject inversion is needed: Scarcely had I reached. The usual pair is scarcely … when, followed here by the simple past the train left.

57.explanation: The final key selects A: each is singular and therefore takes has. The traditional exam version pairs it with his. B also uses singular has and the widely accepted singular their; that modern usage should not be taught as inherently ungrammatical.

58.explanation: The grammatical result construction is so + adjective + that-clause: He is so tired that he cannot walk, option D. The official final key instead lists B, He is very tired that he cannot walk, which lacks the required so. The item is kept unscored while both the official B and independent D are retained for review.

59.explanation: A reported yes/no question uses asked … whether or if plus statement order. Have becomes had after the past reporting verb, and me becomes him, giving Ulysses asked the bird whether it had anything to tell him.

60.explanation: Direct speech restores the speaker’s present-tense I do not wish and changes reported them back to you. The order to go away becomes the imperative go away. Option D preserves both messages; its mismatched closing quote is printed in the paper.

61.explanation: Have often told backshifts to had often told. The original speaker’s me becomes her, and reminded preserves the reference to repeated earlier warnings.

62.explanation: The final key chooses D. Present-perfect direct speech, I have promised and I have kept, can backshift to had promised and had kept in the reported sentence. Reconstructing direct speech from a report can admit other earlier tense contexts, so D is the exam’s chosen reconstruction.

63.explanation: Will becomes would in the reported question, and the yes response is reported as I said that I would. The embedded question has statement order, I would have time.

64.explanation: Under ordinary past-tense backshift, I am going becomes he was going after he said. The pronoun must refer to the original speaker.

65.explanation: The reported question why I was late returns to the direct question Why are you late? Direct questions invert are and you; the reported subject I refers to the person originally addressed as you.

66.explanation: A general truth can retain the present tense in reported speech. Honesty is the best policy therefore remains is, matching the final key’s option A.

1.q: Write a précis of the following passage : (14) Economic inequality is a persistent and growing issue that affects societies worldwide. It refers to the unequal distribution of income, wealth, and opportunities among individuals and groups. While some level of inequality is inevitable in any society, excessive economic disparity can lead to social unrest, reduced economic mobility, and weakened social cohesion. One of the primary drivers of economic inequality is the disparity in education and skills. Individuals with higher levels of education and specialised skills tend to have better job prospects and higher incomes. In contrast, those with limited education and skills often face difficulties in securing well-paying jobs, leading to a widening income gap. This educational inequality is often rooted in socio-economic factors, such as access to quality schools, parental support, and community resources. The labour market also plays a significant role in economic inequality. Technological advancements and globalization have created high-demand, high-paying jobs in certain sectors, while other sectors experience job losses and wage stagnation. This has resulted in a polarized labour market, where a small proportion of workers enjoy significant financial rewards, while many others struggle to make ends meet. Additionally, factors such as gender, race, and ethnicity can further exacerbate labour market inequalities, leading to systemic discrimination and biases. Wealth inequality is another critical aspect of economic disparity. Wealth, which includes assets such as property, investments, and savings, tends to be highly concentrated among a small proportion of the population. This concentration of wealth allows the affluent to generate more income through investments and access better opportunities, perpetuating a cycle of inequality. Conversely, those with little or no wealth have limited financial security and opportunities for upward mobility. Addressing economic inequality requires comprehensive policy interventions. Governments can play a pivotal by implementing progressive taxation, investing in education and skills development, and promoting social safety nets. Progressive taxation ensures that those with higher incomes contribute a fair share to public resources, while investments in education can help bridge the skills gap and provide equal opportunities for all. Social safety nets, such as unemployment benefits and healthcare, can provide financial security and support for those in need. In conclusion, economic inequality is a complex and multifaceted issue that poses significant challenges to social and economic stability. By addressing the root causes of inequality and implementing inclusive policies, we can work towards a more equitable society where all individuals have the opportunity to thrive and contribute to economic growth.

3.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow : There is absolutely no point in complaining that over the years, there has been pressure for increased productivity and higher earnings for workers in industry. There are several ways for increasing employees earnings. Employee earnings can be increased by raising the selling price of the firm’s products and services, reducing profits or costs of raw materials, or augmenting labour productivity. However, increasing employee earning by means other than increased labour productivity jeopardizes the firm’s competitive strength in the market. Higher prices usually mean fewer customer, reduced profit means less capital investment, and low-cost material mean poor product quality. But, increasing labour productivity by enhancing skills and motivation creates an almost unlimited resource. The development of economic resources, human as well as nonhuman, is the product of human effort, and the quality of human effort in large part depends on human motivation.

Enthusing employees with workaholic spirit through traditional authority and financial incentives has become increasingly difficult as employees become economically secure and their dependency on any one particular organization decreases. According to expectancy theorists, the motivation to work increases when an employee feels his performance is an instrument for obtaining desired rewards. Nevertheless, in many organization today employees are entitled to organizational rewards just by being employed. Unions, governmental regulations, and the nature of the job itself in some cases prevent management from relating financial rewards to performance. People may be attracted to join and remain in organizations to receive organizational rewards, but being motivated to join an organization is not the same as being motivated to exert effort in an organization. The challenge to management is to find and administer alternative form of incentives which will induce employees to improve work performance. Such alternative forms of reinforcement will require increased understanding of motivational theories and programmes. 
(i) How can organizations derive maximum advantages?(2) 
(ii) State two things that contribute to an increase in employee earnings according to the passage.(2) 
(iii) How do employees feel motivated to work?(2) 
(iv) Pick out the word from the passage means stimulate or influence.(1) 
(v) What factor determines the quality of human efforts?(2) 
(vi) In the context of the passage, a company’s competitive strength in the market is affected mainly because of _________.(1)

3.explanation: Independent comprehension guide: (i) organizations gain most by improving labour productivity through skills and motivation while maintaining competitive strength; (ii) any two passage methods may be given: higher selling prices, reduced profits or raw-material costs, or greater labour productivity; (iii) expectancy theory says employees work harder when they see their performance as a means of obtaining desired rewards; (iv) induce is a passage word meaning influence or cause someone to act; enthusing is also related to stimulation, so the broad wording permits a supported alternative; (v) the quality of human effort depends largely on human motivation; (vi) complete the blank with increasing earnings by means other than improved labour productivity.
